entries.question: Archer attacks with a [The Scarab God] that was turned face-down by [Ixidron] and Nia blocks with [Scathe Zombies]. Does The Scarab God trigger?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude the die trigger doesn't occur because The Scarab God was face down and had no abilities when the death event was checked.
entries.answer:
No. The face-down The Scarab God has no abilities while it's face down, so nothing triggers when it dies in combat.

What happens: Ixidron's own text ("As this creature enters, turn all other nontoken creatures face down. (They're 2/2 creatures.)") made The Scarab God a face-down 2/2 with no name, no mana cost, and no rules text. When Archer attacks with the face-down The Scarab God and Nia blocks with Scathe Zombies, combat damage is assigned and then dealt simultaneously as a turn-based action that doesn't use the stack [510.2, 703.4m, 120.4b]. Each is a 2/2 dealing 2 damage to the other, so both the face-down The Scarab God and Scathe Zombies are destroyed by lethal damage. Since the dying permanent is a face-down creature with no rules text, its "When The Scarab God dies, return it to its owner's hand at the beginning of the next end step" ability simply isn't on the object to trigger — a triggered ability needs to exist on the object to see its trigger condition [603.1]. Likewise the upkeep ability doesn't exist while it's face down. Any abilities that did trigger on combat damage would go on the stack before the active player receives priority in the combat damage step [510.3a, 120.4b].

Note also that even turning it face up later wouldn't retroactively fix anything: copiable values only revert when the permanent is actually turned face up [708.8]. And this is independent of player count — the same result applies in a two-player game or a multiplayer game, since it depends only on the face-down permanent's characteristics.

Timing caveat: I'm assuming The Scarab God was still face down at the time combat damage was dealt. If it were somehow turned face up before damage (before it died), its copiable values including the dies ability would be restored [708.8], and then its dies trigger would go on the stack after combat damage [510.3a] — and note it would be a 5/5, surviving Scathe Zombies' 2 damage entirely.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. By default, triggered abilities are checked immediately after the event in question to see if they should trigger. However, "leaves-the-battlefield" triggers check the game state immediately before the event instead. At that point, The Scarab God had no abilities.

entries.question: Aminah controls [Shapers' Sanctuary], [Spellskite], and [Feral Krushok]. Nico casts [Pyromatics] targeting Feral Krushok. Aminah activates Spellskite to change the target of Pyromatics to Spellskite. How many times does Shapers' Sanctuary trigger?
entries.reason: The candidate correctly concludes Shapers' Sanctuary triggers twice — once when Pyromatics is cast targeting Feral Krushok and again when Spellskite redirects the target — matching the reference.
entries.answer:
Shapers' Sanctuary triggers twice.

First trigger: Nico casts Pyromatics targeting Feral Krushok. Targets are chosen as part of putting the spell on the stack (115.1), so at that moment Feral Krushok — a creature Aminah controls — becomes the target of a spell an opponent controls, and Shapers' Sanctuary triggers.

Second trigger: when Aminah's Spellskite ability resolves, it changes a target of Pyromatics to Spellskite (115.7b: a "change a target" effect follows the change-target process but only one target may be changed). Spellskite is also a creature Aminah controls, and it newly becomes the target of Pyromatics, which is still a spell Nico controls — so Shapers' Sanctuary triggers again. Note that the trigger condition looks at who controls the spell being targeted (Nico's Pyromatics), not who controls the effect doing the redirecting; Aminah's own Spellskite ability targets Pyromatics, a spell, not a creature, so it doesn't itself cause a trigger.

Each Shapers' Sanctuary trigger lets Aminah draw a card, and each resolves before the spell/ability that caused it (Shapers' Sanctuary ruling #0), so the second draw happens before Pyromatics resolves and deals its 1 damage to Spellskite — and Aminah could even cast a card drawn that way in response (Shapers' Sanctuary ruling #1).

Timing/assumption: I'm assuming Pyromatics was cast without paying its replicate cost, so only one instance of the word "target" exists. If Nico had replicated it, each copy is put on the stack with its own targets (707.10c), and every copy that targets a creature Aminah controls would add another Shapers' Sanctuary trigger. Also, if Spellskite had left the battlefield or otherwise become an illegal target before its ability resolved, no target would change and there'd be no second trigger (Spellskite ruling #1).

This analysis doesn't depend on player count: it works the same at a two-player or multiplayer table, since only Nico's spell and Aminah's permanents are involved.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Twice. Shapers' Sanctuary will trigger the first time when Pyromatics is initially cast targeting Feral Krushok.. Shapers' Sanctuary will trigger again when Spellskite becomes the target of the spell.

entries.question: Anderson plays their land for the turn, then casts a morphed [Zoetic Cavern]. Nataly casts [Delay] targeting Zoetic Cavern on the stack. After that resolves, Anderson casts [Timecrafting] to remove 2 time counters from Zoetic Cavern. After that resolves, Anderson casts Timecrafting to remove the last time counter from Zoetic Cavern. What happens to Zoetic Cavern?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Anderson cannot play Zoetic Cavern when the last time counter is removed because they've already played a land this turn, so it stays exiled (with no time counters).
entries.answer:
Zoetic Cavern stays in exile. Because Anderson has already played a land this turn, they can't play Zoetic Cavern when the last time counter is removed, so it remains exiled — now with no time counters and therefore no longer "suspended."

Step by step:

1. Anderson cast Zoetic Cavern face down using its morph ability, so on the stack it was a face-down 2/2 creature spell with no name, no text, no subtypes and no mana cost, cast for {3} as an alternative cost [702.37c, 708.4].
2. Delay countered that face-down spell and exiled it with three time counters, giving it suspend. Zoetic Cavern is now a suspended card in exile [702.62b, Suspend].
3. Timecrafting's second use is legal: a suspended card with a time counter on it is a legal target, and removing the last time counter triggers suspend's third ability [701.56a, 702.62a].
4. That trigger says its owner "may play it without paying its mana cost if able" [702.62a]. Zoetic Cavern is a land card, and playing a land is a special action that requires an available land play for the turn [116.1]. Anderson already played their land for the turn, so they are not able to play it.
5. Anderson also can't get around this by casting Zoetic Cavern face down again: the morph ability requires paying {3} instead of its mana cost [702.37c], which isn't playing it "without paying its mana cost."

Since Anderson doesn't play it, Zoetic Cavern remains exiled, with zero time counters, and it is no longer suspended (a card is only "suspended" while it has a time counter) — the same end state Delay ruling #11 describes when the trigger doesn't produce a play. Note also that when the last counter is removed the card would be turned face up just before being played, if it could be played [406.3a]; and that the spell is recast/replayed as a brand-new object, with no memory of having been face down [Delay ruling #2].

Timing note: I'm assuming both Timecrafting spells fully resolved before anything else, and that the second one removed the third counter while Anderson's land play for the turn was already used. If Anderson still had a land play available (for example, they hadn't played a land, or an effect granted an extra land play), they could put Zoetic Cavern onto the battlefield face up as a land for free instead. Note also that Timecrafting's {X} is a variable cost — the first one cost {2}{R}, the second {1}{R}.

This works the same whether the game has two players or more; only Zoetic Cavern's owner (Anderson) gets the option to play it.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: It will remain in exile. Suspend allows Anderson to play it, but does not allow Anderson to play additional lands. Since they has already played their land for the turn, they cannot play Zoetic Cavern.

entries.question: Aubree controls an [Opal Acrolith] that is currently a creature and a [Sliver Construct]. They cast [Cytoshape] to turn the Sliver Construct into a copy of Opal Acrolith. Then they activate Sliver Construct's ability to turn it into an enchantment. What happens at the end of turn?
entries.reason: Both conclude Cytoshape's copy effect ends while the activated type-setting effect persists, leaving the permanent as a noncreature enchantment named Sliver Construct with no abilities.
entries.answer:
At end of turn, Cytoshape's copy effect ends and the permanent goes back to being Sliver Construct — but the {0} ability's effect has no duration, so it keeps applying: the permanent ends up as a noncreature enchantment named Sliver Construct, still on the battlefield, with no creature types and no relevant power/toughness.

Why, step by step:

1. Cytoshape resolving: Sliver Construct becomes a copy of Opal Acrolith. It copies Opal Acrolith's copiable values — the printed card, which is just "Enchantment." The earlier effect that had turned Aubree's Opal Acrolith into a 2/4 Soldier creature is a noncopy type-changing effect and is not copied (Cytoshape ruling #0 confirms the copy effect can make the target stop being a creature, copying the printed wording). So Sliver Construct is now an enchantment, not a creature (Opal Acrolith ruling #1 / #2 describe the same either/or).

2. Aubree then activates the copied "{0}: This permanent becomes an enchantment" ability on the Sliver Construct permanent. Note this ability belongs to the permanent itself now, and "this permanent" refers to that object regardless of its current qualities (CR 700.7, CR 707.11). It was already an enchantment, so the activation looks redundant — but its resolution creates a type-setting continuous effect with no duration and a later timestamp than Cytoshape.

3. At the beginning of the end step / as the turn ends, Cytoshape wears off and the permanent reverts to its own copiable values: artifact creature — Sliver Construct, 2/2 (Cytoshape ruling #6). The {0} effect, however, does not wear off. Applying it in layer 4 over those restored values (CR 205.1a: an effect that sets card types replaces the existing card types, and subtypes correlated with a removed card type are also removed) leaves: Enchantment, no artifact or creature type, no Sliver/Construct subtypes. It stays on the battlefield as a permanent (CR 110.4c). Its 2/2 remains as a characteristic but is meaningless while it isn't a creature.

So Aubree is left with an enchantment named Sliver Construct that still has the "{0}: This permanent becomes an enchantment" ability? No — abilities revert with the copy effect, so once Cytoshape ends it has only Sliver Construct's own (absent) abilities; only the type-setting effect it already produced persists (CR 613.6-style continuation of an already-applying effect).

Aubree's original Opal Acrolith is unaffected by any of this and remains a 2/4 Soldier creature.

Timing note: I'm assuming the {0} activation happened after Cytoshape resolved (as stated). If it had somehow been activated before Cytoshape resolved, Cytoshape's later-timestamped copy effect in layer 1 plus the earlier type-setting effect would still leave it an enchantment during the turn, but at end of turn the same {0} effect would still be applying, giving the same final result.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: The effect making Sliver Construct a copy of Opal Acrolith ends, but the effect making it an enchantment does not. It's a noncreature enchantment named "Sliver Construct" with no abilities.

entries.question: Avery controls [Bolas's Citadel] and has [Evermind] on top of their library, can they cast it?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion as the reference: Bolas's Citadel lets Evermind be cast from the top of the library as an alternate-cost casting and Evermind's mana value is 0, so you pay 0 life.
entries.answer:
Yes. Avery can cast Evermind off the top of their library with Bolas's Citadel, and it costs them 0 life.

Why: Bolas's Citadel says "You may play lands and cast spells from the top of your library. If you cast a spell this way, pay life equal to its mana value rather than pay its mana cost." That's an alternative cost — the words "rather than pay its mana cost" mean Avery never pays the mana cost at all, and announcing the intent to use it happens during the proposal step of casting [601.2b]. Because it's a way of casting the card that doesn't involve its (nonexistent) mana cost, it's exactly the sort of "alternate means" that lets Evermind be cast even though Evermind has no printed mana cost [Evermind ruling #2].

The life payment: Evermind's mana value is 0 [Evermind ruling #3], so Avery pays 0 life. Players can always pay 0 life, so there's no resource problem even at 1 life [118.3b].

Timing: Evermind is an instant, so Avery may cast it any time they have priority. Note that while Avery is in the middle of casting Evermind, they can't look at the new top card of their library until the casting is complete [Bolas's Citadel ruling #6].

This works the same in a two-player game and in multiplayer — nothing here depends on the number of opponents. (Splice onto Arcane is irrelevant here: splicing requires revealing Evermind from Avery's hand, not from the top of the library.)

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Normally because Evermind has no mana cost it can't be cast. However Bolas's Citadel is casting it for an alternative cost, and therefore ignores the actual cost of the spell. When calculating the mana value of a spell with no mana cost it's considered zero.

entries.question: Autumn controls [Bolas's Citadel] and has [Sidisi's Pet] on top of their library, can they cast it for its morph cost? If so, how much life will they pay?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line as the reference: Bolas's Citadel applies an alternative cost and morph is an alternative cost, so you cannot combine them and thus can't cast Sidisi's Pet for its morph cost.
entries.answer:
No — Autumn can't use Sidisi's Pet's morph ability off Bolas's Citadel. Bolas's Citadel lets you cast the top card of your library but requires an alternative cost: "pay life equal to its mana value rather than pay its mana cost." Morph is also an alternative cost — "pay {3} rather than pay its mana cost" (702.37a, 702.37c) — and rule 601.2b says a player can't apply two alternative methods of casting or two alternative costs to a single spell. So Autumn must cast Sidisi's Pet face up, paying life equal to its mana value: Sidisi's Pet's mana cost is {3}{B}, mana value 4, so 4 life (no mana at all is paid).

Two clarifications: (1) Morph's {1}{B} on Sidisi's Pet is not a casting cost — it's the cost to turn the face-down permanent face up later as a special action, and only a face-down permanent (never a face-down spell) can be turned face up that way (702.37e, Sidisi's Pet ruling #5, Sidisi's Pet ruling #3). Casting via morph would have cost {3} and made a nameless 2/2 face-down creature spell. (2) Casting a card face down from the top of your library would otherwise be legal zone-wise if a permission allowed it (601.3e, 702.37c), but Bolas's Citadel's mandatory life payment is what blocks combining it with morph here.

This analysis doesn't depend on player count — it's the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table, since only Autumn's own casting permission and costs are involved.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No, they can't cast it. If Autumn uses Bolas's Citadel to cast a spell, they are applying an alternative cost. Morph is also an alternative cost. Only one alternative cost can be applied to a spell when casting it.

entries.question: Ashley controls [Bolas's Citadel] and has [Lovestruck Beast] on top of their library. Can they cast [Heart's Desire]? If so, how much life do they pay?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Ashley can cast Heart's Desire from the top of their library with Bolas's Citadel and will pay 1 life (its mana value) instead of paying {G}.
entries.answer:
Yes — Ashley can cast Heart's Desire, and they pay 1 life rather than {G}.

Why: Bolas's Citadel says "You may play lands and cast spells from the top of your library. If you cast a spell this way, pay life equal to its mana value rather than pay its mana cost." That permission isn't restricted to a card type, so both faces of the adventurer card Lovestruck Beast // Heart's Desire are legal to cast this way. Rule 601.3e covers exactly this: a permission limited to instants and sorceries (Melek, Izzet Paragon) lets you cast only the Adventure half, and a permission limited to creature spells (Garruk's Horde) lets you cast only the creature half — Bolas's Citadel grants both, so Heart's Desire is castable.

The amount of life is set by the mana value of the spell as it exists on the stack. Heart's Desire's mana cost is {G}, so its mana value is 1, and Ashley pays 1 life instead of paying {G}. (If they instead cast the Lovestruck Beast half, whose mana cost is {2}{G}, they'd pay 3 life.) This is an alternative cost replacing the mana cost, so no green mana is spent (118.9, 601.2b, 601.2f); the life payment is locked in as part of the total cost, and any additional costs or cost increases would still apply on top.

After Heart's Desire resolves (creating a 1/1 white Human token), the card goes to exile rather than the graveyard, and Ashley may later cast Lovestruck Beast from exile — at that point it's being cast from exile, not from the top of the library, so Bolas's Citadel's life-payment replacement doesn't apply and they'd pay {2}{G} normally.

Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes and it will cost Ashley 1 life. As part of putting Lovestruck Beast on the stack Ashley chooses whether or not they want to cast the Adventure or not. If they casts Heart's Desire they will need to pay life equal to the mana value of the spell they are casting, which in this case is one.

entries.question: Angelique has [Copy Enchantment] enter the battlefield as a copy of [Estrid's Invocation], which is a copy of [Hardened-Scale Armor]. At the beginning of their next upkeep, which permanents may Angelique exile?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling as the reference: both Copy Enchantment and Estrid's Invocation will have the exile-trigger and Angelique may exile either (or both) of those permanents she controls.
entries.answer:
Angelique may exile her Copy Enchantment, and also Estrid's Invocation itself if she controls it — each of those two permanents' abilities can only exile that same permanent, not the other.

Why Copy Enchantment has the ability: Estrid's Invocation's copy effect includes a modification ("except it has 'At the beginning of your upkeep, you may exile this enchantment...'"), and under rule [707.9b] a characteristic-modifying exception in a copy effect becomes part of the copiable values of the copy. So the Estrid's Invocation on the battlefield has copiable values equal to Hardened-Scale Armor plus that upkeep ability. When Copy Enchantment copies a permanent that is itself copying something, Copy Enchantment enters as whatever that permanent copied ([Copy Enchantment ruling #6], and mirrored by [Estrid's Invocation ruling #9]) — i.e., as Hardened-Scale Armor including the granted upkeep ability. Since Copy Enchantment is now an Aura (Enchant creature, +3/+3), it had to enter attached to a legal creature, chosen as it entered ([Copy Enchantment ruling #1], [303.4d]).

At the beginning of Angelique's upkeep, both triggered abilities trigger (assuming she controls Estrid's Invocation, which copies "an enchantment you control"). Each says "exile this enchantment," and by [201.5a]/[400.7f] that self-reference means only the specific object with the ability. So she may choose to exile either, both, or neither; each exiled one returns to the battlefield under its owner's control as a brand-new object with no memory of what it copied ([400.7]), and must choose a currently-existing enchantment to copy (or nothing) on its way back ([Estrid's Invocation ruling #2], [Estrid's Invocation ruling #7]). Note that a returning Aura-copy again needs a legal creature to enchant, or it goes to the graveyard as a state-based action ([704.5m]).

She may not exile Hardened-Scale Armor itself (the original has no such ability), nor any other player's permanents. This works the same in two-player and multiplayer games, since the trigger is on "your upkeep" and affects only Angelique's own enchantments.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Since both cards will have the ability, either Copy Enchantment and Estrid's Invocation may be exiled.

The copy effect of Estrid's Invocation includes the copy gaining an ability as part of the copying process. This is also a copiable value, and Copy Enchantment will also have this ability.

entries.question: Alessandro controls [Angel's Tomb] and no other creatures. They cast [Mirage Phalanx]. Can they pair it with Angel's Tomb?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the opposite conclusion, claiming you can order simultaneous triggers to make Angel's Tomb a creature before the soulbond resolves and thus be paired, while the reference correctly states the soulbond trigger will not find another creature when Mirage Phalanx enters and pairing cannot occur.
entries.answer:
Yes — provided Alessandro orders the triggers so Angel's Tomb has already become a creature when the soulbond ability resolves.

When Mirage Phalanx enters the battlefield, two abilities trigger at the same time and Alessandro (their controller) chooses the order they go on the stack: Mirage Phalanx's soulbond ability, and Angel's Tomb's triggered ability ("Whenever a creature you control enters, you may have this artifact become a 3/3 white Angel artifact creature with flying until end of turn"). Put the soulbond ability on the stack first and Angel's Tomb's ability on top of it, so Angel's Tomb's ability resolves first and Alessandro chooses to make Angel's Tomb a 3/3 Angel artifact creature. Then the soulbond ability resolves and can pair Mirage Phalanx with Angel's Tomb, since at that moment both are creatures on the battlefield under Alessandro's control [702.95c]. Soulbond only requires "another unpaired creature" — nothing requires it to have been a creature earlier [702.95b].

If instead the soulbond ability resolves first (before Angel's Tomb becomes a creature), Angel's Tomb is still just a noncreature artifact, so it isn't a legal pairing choice and neither permanent becomes paired [702.95c]; the soulbond ability doesn't get a second chance later.

While paired, Mirage Phalanx's static ability gives each of the two paired creatures the combat-beginning token-copy ability. Note also that a creature can be paired with only one other creature [702.95d].

One caveat: Angel's Tomb's animation lasts only until end of turn. The rules supplied here don't include the provision governing whether the pair breaks when Angel's Tomb stops being a creature, so I can't settle that point from this context. This analysis doesn't depend on player count — it works the same in a two-player or multiplayer game.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Soulbond is a triggered ability that will only go on the stack if Alessandro controls another eligible creature when Mirage Phalanx enters the battlefield. However, before Angel's Tomb's ability resolves, Alessandro doesn't control any other eligible creatures.

entries.question: Ariyah controls [The Ozolith] and [Putrid Goblin] with a -1/-1 counter on it. What happens if Putrid Goblin dies?
entries.reason: Both conclude Putrid Goblin's persist doesn't trigger and The Ozolith receives a -1/-1 counter matching the Goblin's, so the candidate reaches the same final ruling.
entries.answer:
Putrid Goblin's persist ability does not trigger, and The Ozolith's first ability triggers and gets one -1/-1 counter placed on it.

Why: persist reads "When this creature dies, if it had no -1/-1 counters on it, return it..." Since Putrid Goblin already had a -1/-1 counter on it when it left the battlefield, that intervening-if condition is false, so persist never triggers ([Putrid Goblin ruling #0] describes the opposite case, where state-based actions had removed the -1/-1 counters via 704.5q/122.3 — that isn't happening here, since there are no +1/+1 counters to pair off).

The Ozolith: "Whenever a creature you control leaves the battlefield, if it had counters on it, put those counters on The Ozolith." Putrid Goblin had a counter, so the ability triggers. Per [The Ozolith ruling #3] and rule 122.8, nothing is literally moved off Putrid Goblin — you instead put the same number and kind of counters (here, one -1/-1 counter) onto The Ozolith. The original counter simply ceases to exist when Putrid Goblin changes zones (122.2, 400.7). If you controlled two copies of The Ozolith, each would get its own -1/-1 counter.

Also note the ordering point in [The Ozolith ruling #3]: even if The Ozolith's trigger resolved first, a leave-the-battlefield ability that checks counters uses the counters that were on the permanent — so The Ozolith's trigger can't "launder" the -1/-1 counter away to enable persist.

Going forward, at the beginning of combat on Ariyah's turn, The Ozolith's second ability may move all counters from The Ozolith onto a target creature — which would put that -1/-1 counter on a creature Ariyah chooses, so be careful what you target.

This answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table; none of the rules involved depend on the number of players.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Putrid Goblin will not return to the battlefield. The Ozolith will have a -1/-1 counter put on it. The Ozolith's ability does not remove counters from the creature, it just puts counters on The Ozolith matching the number and types of counters that the creature had on it when it died. Persist will look back in time to determine if Putrid Goblin had a -1/-1 counter on it at the time it died. Since it did, persist will not trigger.

entries.question: Ares controls [Majestic Auricorn] merged with [Orochi Eggwatcher] on top. They cause Orochi Eggwatcher to flip. What happens?
entries.reason: Both say the merged permanent flips and uses Orochi Eggwatcher's flip-side characteristics while keeping Majestic Auricorn's (non-flip) abilities, so the core ruling is identical.
entries.answer:
The merged permanent flips, and from then on the Orochi Eggwatcher component is represented by its alternative (flip) face — Shidako, Broodmistress.

Details:

- A merged permanent (the result of mutate) is a single permanent represented by all its components, with the top component supplying name, types, power/toughness and other characteristics, plus the abilities of the components under it. Here Orochi Eggwatcher is on top and Majestic Auricorn is under it.
- Rule [730.2h] specifically covers this: if a merged permanent contains a flip card, that component's alternative characteristics are used instead of its normal characteristics when the merged permanent is flipped. So the flip changes the Orochi Eggwatcher component to its Shidako, Broodmistress side.
- Result: one permanent named Shidako, Broodmistress, a legendary Creature — Snake Shaman with base power/toughness 3/3, with the ability "{G}, Sacrifice a creature: Target creature gets +3/+3 until end of turn" from the flipped top component, plus the abilities of Majestic Auricorn from underneath (vigilance and "Whenever this creature mutates, you gain 4 life"). The Orochi Eggwatcher token-making ability no longer applies, since a flipped permanent's normal name, text box, type line, and power/toughness stop applying ([710.2]).
- Flipping is one-way: this permanent can never become unflipped while it remains on the battlefield ([710.4]). Its flipped/unflipped value is one of the four status categories a permanent always has ([110.5]).
- If the flip came from Orochi Eggwatcher's own activated ability, note the ability itself requires you to control ten or more creatures for the flip to happen; the merged permanent counts as only one creature.
- Practical note: because the flipped face is legendary, the "legend rule" applies if Ares controls another Shidako, Broodmistress — that isn't covered by the rules provided here.
- If the merged permanent later leaves the battlefield, one permanent leaves and each component card goes to the appropriate zone, and it retains no memory of its flipped status ([730.3], [710.4]).

Nothing here depends on the number of players, so the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: The merged permanent will flip. The merged permanent will now use Orochi Eggwatcher's flip-side alternate characteristics. This will not affect any abilities the merged permanent has because of Majestic Auricorn, since that component is not a flip card.

entries.question: Nico controls [Vedalken Orrery]. Axl casts [Warrior's Oath]. After it resolves, Nico casts [Trouble in Pairs]. Axl passes the turn. Who takes the next turn?
entries.reason: Both conclude Nico will take the next turn because Trouble in Pairs, if on the battlefield when the extra turn would begin, replaces Axl's extra turn with a skip so Axl never takes it.
entries.answer:
Axl skips the extra turn, so the next turn is taken by the player who would normally follow Axl in turn order — Nico in a two-player game.

Why: Warrior's Oath creates an extra turn for Axl after the current one. Nico's Vedalken Orrery lets Nico cast spells as though they had flash, so Nico can legally cast Trouble in Pairs during Axl's turn. Trouble in Pairs says "If an opponent would begin an extra turn, that player skips that turn instead." The extra turn from Warrior's Oath still exists — it is only skipped at the moment it would begin, and Trouble in Pairs is still on the battlefield at that moment, so Axl never begins it [Trouble in Pairs ruling #2].

A nice side effect for Axl: because Axl never takes that extra turn, the delayed trigger from Warrior's Oath ("At the beginning of that turn's end step, you lose the game") never gets an end step to trigger in, so Axl doesn't lose the game to it.

Timing note: I'm assuming Trouble in Pairs is still on the battlefield when the extra turn would begin. If it left the battlefield before that point (destroyed, bounced, etc.), the extra turn would be unaffected and Axl would take it — and would then lose the game at that turn's end step [Trouble in Pairs ruling #2].

Multiplayer: with more than two players, skipping Axl's extra turn simply means the next player in turn order after Axl (the player to Axl's left, normally) takes the next turn rather than Nico specifically [101.4]. Also, Nico's casting of Trouble in Pairs was legal in the first place because Nico had to receive priority to cast it; a player with priority may cast spells and activate abilities [117.1], and after a spell resolves the active player (Axl) receives priority [117.3b], passing it around the table before anything else resolves [608.1].

entries.question: Amaris controls a [The Flame of Keld] with 2 lore counters on it and [Soul-Scar Mage]. Amaris puts the third lore counter on The Flame of Keld and resolves its final chapter ability. Amaris then casts [Shock], targeting Nico's [River Kaijin]. How many -1/-1 counters are placed on the River Kaijin?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Nico chooses the order of the two replacement effects and that applying The Flame of Keld first yields 4 −1/−1 counters while applying Soul-Scar Mage first yields 2.
entries.answer:
It depends on Nico's choice: either 4 or 2 −1/−1 counters. Nico, as the controller of River Kaijin (the creature that would be dealt the damage), chooses the order in which the two replacement effects are applied.

- If Nico applies The Flame of Keld's chapter III effect first: Shock's 2 damage becomes 2+2 = 4 damage from a red source Amaris controls, then Soul-Scar Mage replaces that noncombat damage with that many −1/−1 counters — 4 counters on River Kaijin, which is enough to kill the 1/4 River Kaijin.
- If Nico applies Soul-Scar Mage first: the 2 damage is replaced with 2 −1/−1 counters, and since no damage is being dealt anymore, The Flame of Keld's "deals that much damage plus 2" effect no longer has a damage event to modify. Result: 2 −1/−1 counters, leaving River Kaijin a 1−2/4−2 = a 0/2 (in effect, a −1/2 that survives as 0/2 power-wise; it isn't destroyed).

This ordering rule is exactly the example given in [Soul-Scar Mage ruling #0]: an opponent may choose to convert the damage into −1/−1 counters before a damage-boosting effect can apply, and then that effect won't apply anymore. Note Soul-Scar Mage's replacement is not a prevention effect ([Soul-Scar Mage ruling #1]), so it works even on unpreventable damage. Also, a replacement effect gets only one chance to apply to an event [614.5], so neither effect re-applies.

Assumptions: I'm assuming chapter III of The Flame of Keld has fully resolved before Shock is cast, as stated; if Shock had already resolved and dealt its damage before chapter III resolved, chapter III would do nothing to that damage at all and only Soul-Scar Mage's 2 counters would apply. Only Nico's River Kaijin is targeted, so nothing here changes between a two-player and a multiplayer game.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: There are two replacement effects trying to apply to the damage being dealt, so Nico chooses which one to apply first. If they apply The Flame of Keld's effect first, Soul-Scar Mage's effect will then apply afterwards, and 4 -1/-1 counters will be placed on the River Kaijin. If they apply the Soul-Scar Mage's effect first, the The Flame of Keld's effect will no longer be applicable and the River Kaijin will only receive 2 -1/-1 counters.

entries.question: Ariel controls [Mana Reflection] and [City of Traitors]. Nico controls [Damping Sphere]. If Ariel taps the City of Traitors for mana, how much mana is produced?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same ruling that Ariel chooses the order of replacement effects and can produce either {C} or {C}{C}, opting for {C}{C}.
entries.answer:
Ariel chooses the order, and she'll choose the order that yields {C}{C} (two colorless mana).

Both Mana Reflection ("If you tap a permanent for mana, it produces twice as much of that mana instead") and Damping Sphere ("If a land is tapped for two or more mana, it produces {C} instead of any other type and amount") are replacement effects that modify the same mana-production event, i.e. the event of tapping City of Traitors for {C}{C} (rules 106.12b, 614.1c). When two or more replacement effects would modify the same event, the affected object's controller chooses one to apply, then re-checks which remain applicable; neither effect gets a second chance at the same event (616.1f, 614.5, and Damping Sphere ruling #2). Here City of Traitors is Ariel's permanent, so Ariel makes the choice.

- Applying Damping Sphere first: City of Traitors is being tapped for two mana, so it produces {C} instead of {C}{C}. Then Mana Reflection applies and doubles it: {C}{C}. Damping Sphere can't apply again to the modified event.
- Applying Mana Reflection first: {C}{C} becomes {C}{C}{C}{C}. Then Damping Sphere applies, since City of Traitors was tapped for two or more mana, replacing all of it with a single {C}.

Since Ariel picks, she picks the first order: {C}{C} — two colorless mana, not generic mana, so it can only pay {C} costs or generic costs.

Note that {C} is colorless mana specifically; it is never a substitute for colored mana. Nothing here depends on the number of players: the choice belongs to Ariel as controller of City of Traitors whether the game has two players or more (616.1f; APNAP order under 101.4/616.1a only matters if multiple players had to make such choices simultaneously).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Either {C} or {C}{C}, Ariel's choice. As the ability resolves, there are two replacement effects attempting to modify it. Ariel chooses which one to apply first. If they apply Mana Reflection first, the event will become "Add {C}{C}{C}{C}" when Damping Sphere then replaces with "Add {C}". If Ariel applies Damping Sphere first, the event becomes "Add {C}", which Mana Reflection then replaces with "Add {C}{C}".

entries.question: Amber controls a [Spellbinder] that exiled [Guardian Angel]. Nico controls a [Meddling Mage] that named "Guardian Angel". As Spellbinder's second ability resolves, what happens?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Spellbinder's ability creates the Guardian Angel copy but Meddling Mage's name prevents it from being cast, so the copy cannot be cast and ceases to exist when the ability finishes resolving.
entries.answer:
Amber may still create the copy, but she can't cast it. Nico's Meddling Mage says "Spells with the chosen name can't be cast," and the copy is a copy of Guardian Angel, so casting it is prohibited.

Details:
- Spellbinder's ability creates a copy of the exiled Guardian Angel card in the exile zone and then gives permission to cast that copy without paying its mana cost [Spellbinder ruling #0], [707.12].
- Casting the copy is still casting a spell, so it requires that no rule or effect prohibit it [601.3], [601.2a]. Meddling Mage's continuous effect prohibits casting spells named Guardian Angel, so Amber simply doesn't get to cast the copy — the "you may cast" permission from Spellbinder can't overcome the prohibition. Note also that Guardian Angel's mana cost is {X}{W}; no choice of X changes its name, so the exception in [601.3a] (choices during proposal that could remove the prohibition) doesn't help here.
- Nothing is countered — the copy is never cast in the first place. A copy that isn't cast doesn't stay around as a playable object; the provided rules don't spell out its disposal, but no Guardian Angel spell ever goes on the stack [112.1a].
- Timing note: if a Guardian Angel copy had somehow already been cast and were on the stack before Meddling Mage entered, Meddling Mage wouldn't affect it [Meddling Mage ruling #1]. Here the order given is that Meddling Mage's naming is already in place when Spellbinder's ability resolves, so the prohibition applies.
- Player count doesn't matter: Meddling Mage's ability applies to spells cast by any player, so the result is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Amber copies the Guardian Angel in exile. Amber can't cast the copy, so it remains in exile. It ceases to exist as soon as Spellbinder's ability finishes resolving.

entries.question: Augustine controls [Butcher Ghoul] enchanted by their [Unhallowed Pact]. They attack with it and Nico blocks with [Scaled Wurm]. Will Butcher Ghoul have a +1/+1 counter when it returns to the battlefield?
entries.reason: Both state Augustine controls and orders the two death triggers, so they can put undying to resolve first to return Butcher Ghoul with a +1/+1 counter.
entries.answer:
It depends on which of Augustine's two triggered abilities Augustine puts on the stack to resolve first — Augustine controls both, so Augustine chooses the order.

When Butcher Ghoul is dealt lethal combat damage by Scaled Wurm and dies, two abilities trigger: Butcher Ghoul's undying ("When this permanent is put into a graveyard from the battlefield, if it had no +1/+1 counters on it, return it to the battlefield under its owner's control with a +1/+1 counter on it" — 702.93a) and Unhallowed Pact's ability ("When enchanted creature dies, return that card to the battlefield under your control"). Unhallowed Pact is put into the graveyard as a state-based action for no longer being attached to a permanent (704.5m), but its ability still finds the card Butcher Ghoul became in the graveyard (400.7e/400.7f, 603.6e).

- If Augustine has undying resolve first: Butcher Ghoul returns to the battlefield with a +1/+1 counter on it. Unhallowed Pact's ability then finds nothing in the graveyard and does nothing (Unhallowed Pact ruling #0, 603.6e).
- If Augustine has Unhallowed Pact's ability resolve first: Butcher Ghoul returns to the battlefield under Augustine's control with no counter, and undying then can't find the card in the graveyard, so it does nothing.

So Augustine can guarantee the +1/+1 counter by ordering undying to resolve first. Note that undying's condition is met here because Butcher Ghoul had no +1/+1 counters on it while on the battlefield; also, any counters a permanent had cease to exist when it changes zones (122.2), so the returning Butcher Ghoul is a new object with only whatever counters the resolving ability gives it.

This analysis doesn't change with more than two players: both triggers are controlled by Augustine, so Augustine alone orders them (APNAP order, 101.4, only matters when different players' choices coincide).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: It's Augustine's choice. There are two triggers when Butcher Ghoul dies, so Augustine can choose the order to put them onto the stack. The first one to resolve will return the Butcher Ghoul to the battlefield, and the second one will do nothing.

entries.question: Aspen attacks with [Aurelia, the Warleader]. Immediately after the trigger resolves, they casts [Time Stop]. Is there an additional combat phase? If so, when?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude there is no additional combat phase because Aurelia’s trigger either would be exiled by Time Stop if still on the stack or, if it already created the extra phase, that scheduled phase is skipped when Time Stop ends the turn.
entries.answer:
No — there is no additional combat phase. Aurelia, the Warleader's trigger did create an additional combat phase after the current one, but Time Stop ends the turn: all spells and abilities on the stack are exiled (including Time Stop itself, which still finishes resolving), all attacking and blocking creatures are removed from combat, the current phase/step ends, and the game skips straight to the cleanup step, skipping every phase and step in between [724.1d] [Time Stop ruling #3]. The extra combat phase Aurelia, the Warleader would have added lies between the current combat phase and the cleanup step, so it is simply skipped — to skip a phase is to proceed past it as though it didn't exist [500.11] [614.10b].

Timing assumption: you said Time Stop was cast and resolved after Aurelia, the Warleader's attack trigger had already resolved, so the extra combat phase was already scheduled. It doesn't matter — an already-scheduled but not-yet-started phase can still be skipped [614.10b]. If instead Time Stop had resolved while the Aurelia, the Warleader trigger was still on the stack, that trigger would have been exiled and never created the extra phase at all [Time Stop ruling #3]; either way, no additional combat phase occurs.

Also note Aurelia, the Warleader gives only an extra combat phase, not an extra main phase [Aurelia, the Warleader ruling #0], and that extra phase would have been inserted directly after the current combat phase [500.8]. Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

One practical note: any abilities that trigger during this ending process go on the stack during the cleanup step, and players then get priority before a second cleanup step [Time Stop ruling #2]. "At the beginning of the end step" abilities won't trigger this turn [Time Stop ruling #1].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: There is no additional combat phase. When Aurelia, the Warleader's trigger resolves, it adds the phase to the structure of the current turn. When Time Stop resolves, it skips all remaining steps and phases until the cleanup step.

entries.question: In Aspen's draw step, they tap [Vault of Catlacan] for 8 blue mana and cast [Time Stop]. Aspen discards a [Guile] to hand size. Can they use the two remaining {U} to cast an instant?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes an instant can be cast (a window opens), directly contradicting the reference's ruling that the mana emptied and no spell can be cast.
entries.answer:
Direct answer: Yes — a window to cast an instant does open, because discarding Guile causes a triggered ability. But whether the two floating {U} are still available in that window isn't settled by the rules provided here.

Why the window exists: Time Stop's effect ends the turn. During that process no player gets priority and triggered abilities are not put onto the stack [724.1f]. The exile of spells and the active player's discard to maximum hand size all happen inside that process. Discarding Guile puts it into Aspen's graveyard, and Guile's own text says "When Guile is put into a graveyard from anywhere, shuffle it into its owner's library" — that's a triggered ability that has triggered during the end-the-turn process. Because at least one triggered ability triggered, it is put onto the stack during the cleanup step, then the active player (Aspen) gets priority and players may cast spells and activate abilities [724.1f], [514.3a]. So Aspen (and each opponent, in any player count — this part works the same at two players or more, with priority passing in turn order) can cast an instant during that cleanup step. Afterward the stack empties, all players pass, and another cleanup step begins before the turn actually ends [724.1f], [514.3a]. Had nothing triggered, no player would have received priority at all and no instant could be cast [514.3].

The mana caveat: the rules excerpts given do not include the rule about mana pools emptying at the end of each step and phase, so I can't confirm from this context that the 2 remaining blue mana from Vault of Catlacan survives from the draw step into the cleanup step. If that mana has emptied, Aspen would need new mana — and Vault of Catlacan is already tapped. Treat the 8 blue as spent on Time Stop's {4}{U}{U} (which is 4 generic plus two blue specifically) with 2 blue left over only for as long as mana persists.

Timing note: I'm assuming Time Stop resolved and the discard happened as part of ending the turn (that's how Time Stop works). If instead Guile had been put into the graveyard before the end-the-turn process began, its shuffle trigger would already have been on the stack and exiled by Time Stop, and then — with no ability having triggered during the process — no player would get priority in the cleanup step and no instant could be cast [724.1f], [514.3].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. The mana was removed from the mana pool when the draw step ended.

entries.question: Alex controls an [Oracle of Mul Daya] and has played 2 lands this turn. They casts [Flicker], targeting the Oracle of Mul Daya. After if resolves, can they play a 3rd land?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion — Flickering doesn't reset or add to the per-turn land allowance, Oracle of Mul Daya grants a total of two land plays and Alex has already used both.
entries.answer:
No — Alex cannot play a third land.

Alex's land allowance is 1 (the normal land play) + 1 from Oracle of Mul Daya's static ability, for a total of 2, and Alex has already played 2 lands this turn. Flickering Oracle of Mul Daya doesn't reset or add to that count. To determine legality you compare the number of lands the player may play this turn with the number already played this turn; if the allowance isn't greater, the play is illegal (305.2a, 305.2b).

Why the exile-and-return doesn't help:
- Oracle of Mul Daya's ability is a continuous effect from a static ability, which isn't "locked in" and simply applies at any given moment to whatever its text says (611.3a). At the moment after Flicker resolves, Alex controls one Oracle of Mul Daya, so the allowance is still 2 total — not 3.
- The returned permanent is technically a new object with no memory of its previous existence (400.7i), but the count of lands Alex has already played is tracked per player, not per permanent, so it stays at 2.
- Only controlling multiple Oracle of Mul Daya at once stacks: with two on the battlefield you could play three lands (Oracle of Mul Daya ruling #0). Flicker returns the same single creature, so no stacking occurs.

If Alex wants a third land play, they need a second Oracle of Mul Daya (or another additional-land effect) on the battlefield before making the play. Note also that Oracle of Mul Daya's third ability only changes where lands can be played from (the top of the library), not how many or when — such a play still uses one of Alex's land plays for the turn (Oracle of Mul Daya ruling #2).

This analysis is independent of player count; nothing here changes between a two-player game and a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Alex has 1 land play this turn by default, which Oracle of Mul Daya increase to 2. Alex has already played 2 lands this turn, so no more lands can be played.

entries.question: Ariel controls [Bastion Inventor] and an [Oblivion Ring] that exiled Noelle's [Ghostly Possession]. Noelle casts [Serene Offering] targeting Oblivion Ring. What happens as the Ghostly Possession returns to the battlefield?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Oblivion Ring's return attaches Ghostly Possession to Bastion Inventor without targeting, so Bastion Inventor's hexproof doesn't prevent it.
entries.answer:
Serene Offering destroys Oblivion Ring; Oblivion Ring's leave-the-battlefield trigger returns Ghostly Possession to the battlefield under its owner's control (Noelle's), and Noelle — as the returning Aura's owner/controller — chooses a creature for it to enchant as it enters. Because this return doesn't target, Bastion Inventor's hexproof does NOT protect it: Noelle may legally attach Ghostly Possession to Ariel's Bastion Inventor, giving it flying and preventing all combat damage it would deal or be dealt.

Details:
- Oblivion Ring's second ability returns the exiled card, and the ruling for Oblivion Ring states that if the exiled card is an Aura, its owner chooses what it enchants; the Aura doesn't target, but its enchant ability still restricts legal choices [Oblivion Ring ruling #2].
- This matches the general Aura rule: an Aura entering the battlefield by means other than resolving as an Aura spell, with no object specified by the effect, has its controller choose a legal object per its enchant ability [303.4f].
- Ghostly Possession says "Enchant creature," so any creature on the battlefield is a legal choice. Bastion Inventor's hexproof only stops it being "the target of spells or abilities your opponents control" — no targeting occurs here, so it is a legal choice.
- If there were no creature at all on the battlefield, Ghostly Possession would have no legal object and would remain in exile forever [Oblivion Ring ruling #2], [303.4g].
- After it's attached, if it ever becomes attached to an illegal object or nothing, it goes to Noelle's graveyard as a state-based action [704.5m], [303.4c].

Timing note: I'm assuming Serene Offering resolves and destroys Oblivion Ring after Oblivion Ring's exile ability had already resolved. If instead Oblivion Ring left the battlefield before its first ability resolved, the return trigger would do nothing and Ghostly Possession would be exiled permanently [Oblivion Ring ruling #0].

Multiplayer: the same result holds with more than two players; the only added restriction is that an Aura can't enchant something outside its controller's range of influence [801.8].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: It enchants Bastion Inventor. Auras entering the battlefield from a zone other than the stack must enchant a legal object. It doesn't target anything, so hexproof doesn't matter.

entries.question: Ainsley controls [Everlasting Torment] and casts [Soul Burn] with X = 2 targeting Nixon's [Forest Bear]. (Spending {B}{B}{B}{B}{B}.) How much life does Ainsley gain?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Ainsley gains 0 life (the candidate reaches the same final ruling, despite differing/incorrect intermediate reasoning).
entries.answer:
Ainsley gains 0 life. Everlasting Torment says "Players can't gain life," and that printed text overrides the life-gain clause of Soul Burn — a card's own text wins over the general rule that a spell's instructions are carried out, so the "You gain life equal to the damage dealt" portion simply does nothing (an instruction that can't be carried out is ignored, per [615.6]).

What does happen: Soul Burn with X = 2 deals 2 damage to Nixon's Forest Bear (a 2/2). Because Everlasting Torment also says "All damage is dealt as though its source had wither," that damage is dealt to Forest Bear in the form of two -1/-1 counters instead of marked damage, making it 0/0, so Forest Bear is put into its owner's graveyard.

Note also Everlasting Torment's "Damage can't be prevented": if anything tried to prevent this damage, the prevention effect would still be applied but would prevent nothing, though any additional effects it has would still occur ([615.12a]). Since Soul Burn's life gain is capped at the unprevented damage dealt ([Soul Burn ruling #0]) and here nothing is prevented, the cap would have been 2 — but Everlasting Torment reduces the actual gain to nothing. Rule [119.10] confirms that a life-gain event that would be 0 simply doesn't occur.

Spending five {B} on X doesn't matter beyond the cap: X was chosen as 2, so only 2 damage is dealt regardless of how much black mana was spent (extra black mana would only have raised the life-gain cap, which is moot here). This answer doesn't depend on the number of players at the table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: 0. The instructions of the spell are carried out in order. By the time Ainsley would gain life, the creature's toughness has been reduced to 0 by the -1/-1 counters, so they can't gain more than 0 life.

entries.question: Andy controls 3 artifacts and casts [Rusted Relic]. Neriah controls [Imposing Sovereign]. Does Rusted Relic enter the battlefield tapped or untapped?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion — Rusted Relic is a creature as it enters due to metalcraft, so Imposing Sovereign's replacement effect causes it to enter tapped.
entries.answer:
Rusted Relic enters the battlefield tapped.

Why: when checking replacement effects that modify how a permanent enters the battlefield, you look at the permanent's characteristics as it would exist on the battlefield, including continuous effects from its own static abilities that would apply once it's there, plus continuous effects that already exist and would apply to it ([614.12], [614.12a], [611.3c]). Rusted Relic's metalcraft ability is a static ability that makes it a 5/5 Golem artifact creature as long as its controller controls three or more artifacts. Andy already controls 3 artifacts, and Rusted Relic itself counts once on the battlefield, so the condition is met and Rusted Relic is a creature as it enters 
oncreature artifact that only later turns into a creature. Characteristic-setting continuous effects apply simultaneously with the permanent entering, not after ([611.3c]).

Because Rusted Relic is therefore a creature Neriah's opponent (Andy) controls as it enters, Imposing Sovereign's replacement effect "Creatures your opponents control enter tapped" applies ([614.1d] \u2014 "[Objects] enter [the battlefield] . . ." effects are replacement effects), and Rusted Relic enters tapped.

Notes: If Andy did not control three or more artifacts counting Rusted Relic, Rusted Relic would enter as a noncreature artifact and Imposing Sovereign would not tap it. Also, Rusted Relic being tapped doesn't stop it from being a 5/5; and per [Rusted Relic ruling #0], summoning sickness depends on how long Andy has controlled it, not how long it has been a creature. This analysis is the same whether the game has two players or more \uares that Neriah is an opponent of Andy; in a multiplayer game only creatures controlled by Imposing Sovereign's controller's opponents are affected.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Tapped. To determine what replacement effects apply to a permanent as it enters the battlefield, the game looks at the permanent as it would exist on the battlefield. On the battlefield Rusted Relic would be a creature, so Imposing Sovereign's effect will apply to it.

entries.question: Nathaniel controls [Pithing Needle] naming [Skullsnatcher]. Alex has Skullsnatcher in their hand and declares an attack with [Borderland Minotaur]. Nathaniel declares no blockers. Can Alex use ninjutsu to put Skullsnatcher onto the battlefield?
entries.reason: Both conclude Alex cannot use Skullsnatcher's ninjutsu because it is an activated ability and Pithing Needle naming Skullsnatcher prevents activating that ability.
entries.answer:
No. Alex cannot activate Skullsnatcher's ninjutsu ability while Nathaniel's Pithing Needle names Skullsnatcher.

Why: Ninjutsu is an activated ability, not a triggered or static one — "Ninjutsu {B}" means "{B}, Reveal this card from your hand, Return an unblocked attacking creature you control to its owner's hand: Put this card onto the battlefield from your hand tapped and attacking" [702.49a]. It's an activated ability that functions from Alex's hand because its cost can only be paid there [113.6j]. Pithing Needle says activated abilities of sources with the chosen name can't be activated unless they're mana abilities; ninjutsu produces no mana, so it isn't a mana ability. Pithing Needle applies regardless of the zone the named card is in, including hand [Pithing Needle ruling #0]. A player can't begin to activate an ability that's prohibited from being activated [602.5], so Alex can't even announce it or reveal Skullsnatcher.

So Borderland Minotaur simply stays unblocked and deals its combat damage (4) to Nathaniel; Skullsnatcher remains in Alex's hand. Alex could still cast Skullsnatcher normally for {1}{B} at a later legal time (casting is not activating an ability), though Skullsnatcher's own combat-damage triggered ability, being triggered, wouldn't be stopped by Pithing Needle either [603.2a]. If Pithing Needle later leaves the battlefield, ninjutsu becomes activatable again [Pithing Needle ruling #3].

This answer doesn't depend on player count: the same result holds in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table, as long as Pithing Needle is within Alex's range of influence [801.6] and Alex's attacker is unblocked by whichever player is the defending player.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Ninjutsu is an activated ability.

entries.question: Azariah controls [Magus of the Moon] and plays [Three Tree City]. Do they make a choice for it as it enters? If not, what happens if Magus of the Moon leaves the battlefield later?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that Magus of the Moon makes Three Tree City enter as a Mountain so it has no "as it enters" choice and later removal of Magus doesn't retroactively allow that choice — a choice can only occur if it actually enters without Magus's effect.
entries.answer:
No — Azariah makes no choice as Three Tree City enters, and no choice can be made later.

Why: Magus of the Moon's static ability says "Nonbasic lands are Mountains," which sets Three Tree City's land subtype to Mountain, and setting a land's subtype this way replaces its old land types and its printed mana abilities (it just has "{T}: Add {R}"). Continuous effects that modify a permanent's characteristics apply simultaneously with the permanent entering the battlefield, not after — the permanent is never on the battlefield with unmodified characteristics [611.3c] [603.6b]. When you determine which "as this enters" replacement effects apply, you check the characteristics of the permanent as it would exist on the battlefield, taking existing continuous effects into account [614.12] [614.12a]. So as Three Tree City enters, it is a Mountain that doesn't have "As Three Tree City enters, choose a creature type," and that replacement effect simply never applies. This is the same logic as the 603.6b example where an effect saying "All creatures lose all abilities" stops an entering creature's ETB ability from triggering, and as the Essence of the Wild example in [616.1f], where a copy effect strips away the entering-tapped ability.

"As [this permanent] enters..." text is a static ability generating a replacement effect [614.1c] [603.6d], and it functions only as that object is entering the battlefield [113.6h]. Therefore, if Magus of the Moon later leaves the battlefield, Three Tree City goes back to being a Legendary Land with its printed abilities, including "{T}: Add {C}" and the {2}, {T} ability — but it is already on the battlefield, so the "as it enters" choice does not happen retroactively and there is no window to make it. Three Tree City has no chosen creature type. Its {2}, {T} ability can still be activated (you choose a color), but since no creature type was ever chosen, the count of creatures you control of the chosen type is zero, so it adds no mana. To get a creature type chosen, Three Tree City would have to enter the battlefield again (e.g., be returned to hand and replayed) while no Magus of the Moon effect is applying.

This works the same regardless of player count; nothing here depends on the number of players. If multiple such replacement effects needed ordering, choices would be made in APNAP order [101.4] [616.1], but that isn't the case here.

One note on Magus of the Moon: even if Magus of the Moon loses its abilities, it keeps turning nonbasic lands into Mountains, because subtype-changing effects are applied before ability-removing effects [Magus of the Moon ruling #0]. The rules text quoted above doesn't include the specific land-subtype rule (305.7) spelling out that setting a land's subtype removes its other land types and printed mana abilities; that step is standard and is what makes Three Tree City lack its "as it enters" ability here.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
No. Making a choice for Three Tree City as it enters is a replacement effect. When determining which replacement effects apply to Three Tree City as it's entering the battlefield, the game looks at how it will exist on the battlefield after it enters. On the battlefield Three Tree City is a Mountain, and Mountains don't make choices as they enter.

If the Magus of the Moon leaves the battlefield later on, Three Tree City is not entering the battlefield again, so it will simply have had no choice made for it.

entries.question: Ari attacks with [Suntail Hawk]. Nayeli casts [Vault Skyward] to give [Brimaz, King of Oreskos] flying until end of turn and blocks Suntail Hawk. Will the token created by Brimaz, King of Oreskos also be blocking Suntail Hawk?

Likewise, Suntail Hawk already became a blocked creature when Brimaz, King of Oreskos was declared, so the token entering doesn't re-trigger "becomes blocked" abilities (509.3c).

entries.question: Aryan splice [Evermind] onto [Barrel Down Sokenzan]. Can they target [Phyrexian Crusader] with the spliced spell?

No. Phyrexian Crusader can't be targeted by the spliced spell, because Barrel Down Sokenzan is a red spell and Phyrexian Crusader has protection from red and from white — protection means it can't be targeted by spells with the stated quality (702.16b), and "protection from red and from white" works as two separate protection abilities (702.16i).

Splicing Evermind onto Barrel Down Sokenzan doesn't help here for two reasons:

1. Splice only adds the spliced card's rules text; the spell keeps its own name, mana cost, and color (702.47c, 612.10). So the resulting spell is still red Barrel Down Sokenzan, not blue. (The Glacial Ray/Reach Through Mists example in 702.47c is the reverse case — there the main spell was blue, so protection from red didn't stop it.)
2. Evermind's added text is just "Draw a card," which has no target at all. It adds no new instance of the word "target," so there's nothing on the spliced spell that could legally point at Phyrexian Crusader. Targets for added text would be chosen normally after revealing the spliced card, and each instance of "target" can get its own choice (702.47d, 601.2b, 601.2c, Evermind ruling #5) — but here the only "target" is Barrel Down Sokenzan's damage target, which Phyrexian Crusader is immune to.

So Aryan must choose some other creature as the target of the damage; if no other creature is a legal target, Barrel Down Sokenzan can't be cast at all. (Aryan can still splice Evermind onto a different Arcane spell later, since Evermind stays in hand — 702.47a.) Also note: if Phyrexian Crusader somehow became a legal target when cast and gained protection from red before resolution, the spell wouldn't resolve at all if that were its only target, meaning the spliced "Draw a card" wouldn't happen either (608.2b, 702.47d).

This analysis doesn't depend on player count — protection works the same at a two-player or multiplayer table.

entries.answer_gold: No. Evermind has a color indicator that makes it blue, and that will not be spliced onto Barrel Down Sokenzan because it's not a part of its text box.

entries.question: Armani controls [Soul Echo] with 0 counters on it and Nico controls [Spirit of the Hearth]. Will Armani have to sacrifice Soul Echo at the beginning of their upkeep?
entries.reason: The reference states the upkeep trigger will not be put on the stack (so Soul Echo is not sacrificed), while the candidate adds a multiplayer exception and therefore does not give the same unconditional ruling.
entries.answer:
Short answer: it depends on whether Nico is Armani's only opponent.

• Two-player game (Armani vs. Nico only): Soul Echo's triggered ability reads "At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice this enchantment if there are no echo counters on it. Otherwise, target opponent may choose..." — the ability requires a target opponent. Spirit of the Hearth gives its controller Nico hexproof ("You have hexproof"), so Nico can't be the target of spells or abilities Armani's opponents control — i.e., of Armani's ability. With no legal target available, Armani's trigger can't be put on the stack with a legal target and never resolves, so Soul Echo is not sacrificed even though it has 0 echo counters.

• Multiplayer with at least one other opponent who doesn't have hexproof: Armani must choose that player as the target, the ability resolves, and because Soul Echo has no echo counters on it Armani sacrifices Soul Echo. The "otherwise" damage-replacement clause never comes up.

Caveats and grounding: the conclusion for the two-player case rests on the general targeting rule that an ability with no legal targets is removed from the stack, which was not included in the rules context provided to me, so treat that half as reasoning from Spirit of the Hearth's card text rather than a cited rule. What is fully grounded is that Soul Echo's upkeep trigger targets an opponent and that hexproof stops Armani from targeting Nico, and that when the ability does resolve with 0 echo counters, Soul Echo is sacrificed. Note also that this sacrifice comes from a triggered ability that uses the stack, not from a state-based action, so it happens on resolution of the trigger, not automatically (compare the automatic, non-stack state-based actions in rules 704.1 and 117.5).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Since the ability has no legal targets, it would trigger at the beginning of the upkeep but would not be put on the stack.

entries.question: Addison controls [The Book of Vile Darkness], and token copies of [Eye of Vecna] and [Hand of Vecna] created by [Saheeli's Artistry]. Addison then activates The Book of Vile Darkness. What abilities will the Vecna token have?
entries.reason: The candidate incorrectly states the Vecna token has no triggered abilities, while the correct ruling is that it does gain The Book of Vile Darkness's end-step trigger (it just doesn't gain abilities from the exiled tokens).
entries.answer:
Addison gets Vecna as a plain legendary 8/8 black Zombie God creature token with indestructible and no triggered abilities.

Why: The activation cost of The Book of Vile Darkness is "{T}, Exile The Book of Vile Darkness and artifacts you control named Eye of Vecna and Hand of Vecna." The token copies made by Saheeli's Artistry do have the names Eye of Vecna and Hand of Vecna, because a token that's a copy of an object takes that object's name as a copiable value [707.2, 111.4], so they are legal to exile for the cost and the ability can be activated.

However, the ability grants Vecna "all triggered abilities of the exiled cards," and a ruling on The Book of Vile Darkness confirms that the ability looks at the cards in exile, not at permanents on the battlefield [The Book of Vile Darkness ruling #2]. Token copies of Eye of Vecna and Hand of Vecna are tokens, not cards, and once they leave the battlefield to exile there are no cards named Eye of Vecna or Hand of Vecna in exile for the ability to look at. The Book of Vile Darkness itself is an artifact card, but it has no triggered ability other than its own end-step ability — and it isn't named Eye of Vecna or Hand of Vecna; the granting clause covers the exiled cards, and the only card exiled here is The Book of Vile Darkness itself, so Vecna would at most pick up The Book of Vile Darkness's own end-step trigger ("At the beginning of your end step, if you lost 2 or more life this turn, create a 2/2 black Zombie creature token"), and nothing from the two token copies.

So in particular Vecna will not have Eye of Vecna's enters-the-battlefield draw/lose-2-life trigger or upkeep trigger (which would otherwise be copiable and would trigger, per [The Book of Vile Darkness ruling #0]), and not Hand of Vecna's beginning-of-combat pump trigger.

Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Only indestructible and "At the beginning of your end step, if you lost 2 or more life this turn, create a 2/2 black Zombie creature token.". It won't get the abilities of the exiled tokens, because they're not cards.

entries.question: Aspen casts [Buried Alive] while controlling [Extus, Oriq Overlord]. Can they put [Virulent Sliver] into their graveyard with Buried Alive, and return it with Extus, Oriq Overlord's triggered ability?

Extus, Oriq Overlord's Magecraft ability triggers when Buried Alive is *cast*, so the trigger goes on the stack on top of Buried Alive and its target is chosen at that moment. At that time Virulent Sliver is still in Aspen's library, not their graveyard, so it isn't a legal target. Magecraft also resolves *before* Buried Alive resolves.

What Aspen can do: choose as the Magecraft target any nonlegendary creature card already in their graveyard when the trigger is put on the stack. If there is no such card at all, the Magecraft ability simply has no legal target and is removed from the stack; Buried Alive then resolves and searches up to three creature cards (Virulent Sliver among them) into the graveyard, where they'll sit until some later spell or copy triggers Magecraft again.

A note on the sequencing you might be assuming: if instead you imagined casting a second instant or sorcery after Buried Alive had already resolved, that new Magecraft trigger could legally target Virulent Sliver in the graveyard and return it to hand, since Virulent Sliver is a nonlegendary creature card.

This interaction is the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table — nothing about Magecraft or Buried Alive depends on the number of opponents.

entries.answer_gold: No. Extus, Oriq Overlord triggers when Aspen casts Buried Alive, and will go on the stack above it. At this point, a legal target has to be chosen. The ability will then resolve before the spell that caused it to trigger does.

entries.question: Aiyana casts [Murktide Regent], exiling 5 instants. In response, Nico casts [Dress Down]. How many +1/+1 counters will Murktide Regent enter the battlefield with?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Murktide Regent enters with zero +1/+1 counters because Dress Down is on the battlefield when its replacement effect is checked, so the enters-with-counters ability isn't present to apply.
entries.answer:
Murktide Regent enters the battlefield with zero +1/+1 counters.

Why: Nico's Dress Down was cast in response to Murktide Regent, so Dress Down is above Murktide Regent on the stack and resolves first [117.7], [608.1]. Once Dress Down has resolved, its static ability "Creatures lose all abilities" is a continuous effect that already exists when Murktide Regent starts to enter the battlefield.

Murktide Regent's "This creature enters with a +1/+1 counter on it for each instant and sorcery card exiled with it" is a replacement effect that modifies how it enters the battlefield [614.1c]. To decide which such replacement effects apply, you check Murktide Regent's characteristics as it would exist on the battlefield, taking into account continuous effects that already exist and would apply to it [614.12a]. Continuous effects that modify a permanent's characteristics apply simultaneously with it entering, not after [611.3c]. Because Dress Down's effect strips Murktide Regent of all abilities as it enters, the "enters with a +1/+1 counter" ability isn't there to apply, and no counters are placed. Likewise its flying and its triggered ability don't function while Dress Down is on the battlefield; when Dress Down is sacrificed at the beginning of the end step, Murktide Regent gets its abilities back but does not retroactively gain the counters it missed, since replacement effects can't go back and change an event that has already happened [614.4]. It will be a 3/3.

Cost note: delve let Aiyana exile 5 instants to pay the {5} generic portion; she still had to pay {U}{U}, and Murktide Regent's mana value remains 7 [Murktide Regent ruling #0].

This works the same whether the game has two players or more — the only thing that matters is that Dress Down resolved before Murktide Regent did. (If instead Dress Down had been cast after Murktide Regent already resolved and was on the battlefield, Murktide Regent would have entered with 5 counters, kept them as counters aren't removed by losing abilities, and simply have no abilities while Dress Down remains.)

entries.answer_gold: Zero. When determining how to apply Murktide Regent's replacement effect, its characteristics are checked as it would exist on the battlefield. Since Dress Down is on the battlefield, Murktide Regent would have no abilities while on the battlefield, so its replacement effect won't apply.

entries.question: Nathaniel controls [Dryad Militant]. Armani casts [Hanabi Blast]. Does it return to their hand?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling — Hanabi Blast returns to its owner's hand during resolution and is never put into a graveyard, so Dryad Militant's replacement effect does not apply.
entries.answer:
Yes — Hanabi Blast returns to its owner's hand, and Nathaniel's Dryad Militant does nothing to stop it.

Why: Dryad Militant's ability is a replacement effect that only applies "If an instant or sorcery card would be put into a graveyard from anywhere" ([614.3], [616.2]). Hanabi Blast's own text returns it from the stack to its owner's hand as part of its resolution, so it never would be put into a graveyard, and Dryad Militant's replacement effect has no event to replace.

Ownership: it goes to the hand of Hanabi Blast's owner, not necessarily Armani's hand. Per [400.3], a card that would go to a hand other than its owner's goes to its owner's hand instead, and per [Hanabi Blast ruling #0], if another player casts a Hanabi Blast that you own, it returns to your hand and then the caster (Armani) discards a card at random. Assuming Armani owns the copy they cast, it returns to Armani's hand.

The one place Dryad Militant matters: the random discard. If the card Armani discards is an instant or sorcery card, Dryad Militant exiles it instead of letting it reach the graveyard. It still counts as discarded, so madness and similar discard-triggered abilities work, and effects that look at the discarded card can find it in exile ([Dryad Militant ruling #0]). Notably, if the randomly discarded card is the just-returned Hanabi Blast, that Hanabi Blast is exiled rather than put into the graveyard.

This works the same with two players or more than two — Dryad Militant's ability applies to instant and sorcery cards owned by any player, and only the caster (Armani) discards.
