entries.answer_gold: Yes. Resolving spells do not leave the stack until they finish resolving. Returning the Hanabi Blast to its owner's hand is part of its resolution, so it is never put into exile.

entries.question: In a two-player game, Ally casts [Rushblade Commander]. Can they attack with it this turn?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion that Rushblade Commander gives itself haste (since "your team" is just you in a two‑player game) and so can attack that turn if it entered before attackers were declared.
entries.answer:
Yes. Rushblade Commander is itself a Warrior (Creature — Azra Warrior), and its own ability says "Warriors your team controls have haste," so Rushblade Commander gives itself haste and can attack the turn it comes down.

Why: normally the "summoning sickness" rule stops a creature from attacking (or activating abilities with {T} or {Q} in the cost) unless it has been under its controller's control continuously since the beginning of that player's most recent turn [302.6]. Haste turns that off: a creature with haste can attack even if its controller hasn't controlled it continuously since their most recent turn began [702.10b], and its {T}/{Q} abilities can be activated right away too [702.10c]. When declaring attackers, each chosen creature must be untapped and must either have haste or have been controlled since the turn began [508.1a] — Rushblade Commander satisfies the haste clause.

Note this is a static ability that applies as soon as Rushblade Commander is on the battlefield, so no waiting is needed. This works the same in a two-player game as at a multiplayer table; in formats with teams, the ability also grants haste to Warriors your teammates control ("your team controls"), which is card text beyond the general rules quoted here.

Assumption: Rushblade Commander resolved before your declare attackers step (e.g., cast in your main phase); if it somehow entered after the declare attackers step, haste wouldn't help — there would be no attacker declaration left this turn.

entries.answer_gold: Yes. In a two-player game, "your team" means "you".

entries.question: Alberto casts [Parch] with its second mode, targeting Nico's [Kasimir the Lone Wolf]. In response, Nico casts [Prismatic Lace], choosing red. What happens when Parch resolves?

entries.answer:
Parch doesn't resolve at all. Alberto chose the mode "Parch deals 4 damage to target blue creature," so the target must be a blue creature. Prismatic Lace makes Kasimir the Lone Wolf "the color or colors of your choice" — Nico chose red only, so Kasimir the Lone Wolf is now mono-red and is no longer blue (Prismatic Lace sets the colors rather than adding one, and this effect lasts indefinitely).

When Parch tries to resolve, it rechecks its target's legality. Because a change to the game state (its characteristics — here, its color) has made Kasimir the Lone Wolf an illegal target, and it was Parch's only target, Parch doesn't resolve: it's removed from the stack and put into Alberto's graveyard [608.2b]. No damage is dealt to Kasimir the Lone Wolf. Note Alberto can't switch to the other mode (2 damage to any target) — modes are locked in when the spell is cast.

Kasimir the Lone Wolf stays on the battlefield unharmed and remains red until something else changes its color; the color change from Prismatic Lace persists independently of Parch [611.2c]. This answer doesn't depend on the number of players at the table.

entries.answer_gold: The Kasimir the Lone Wolf is now a mono-red permanent; it is no longer blue. The game checks to see if its targets are still legal. Kasimir the Lone Wolf is no longer a legal target for Parch, so it is removed from the stack and doesn't resolve.

entries.question: Alfonso has 20 life and has cast a [Channel] previously this turn. Nancy casts [Word of Command], choosing [Squire] from Alfonso's hand. Can Nancy have Alfonso pay 20 life to add 20 colorless mana while casting the Squire, causing Alfonso to lose the game?
entries.reason: The candidate incorrectly treats Channel as a mana ability barred by Word of Command, while the reference ruling correctly states Channel is a special action and may be used to add mana to cast the chosen spell.
entries.answer:
No. Word of Command's own text says that while the controlled player is playing the chosen card, "the player can activate mana abilities only if they're from lands that player controls and only if mana they produce is spent to activate other mana abilities of lands the player controls and/or to play that card." Channel's ability is a mana ability, but it is not a mana ability of a land Alfonso controls — it's a floating effect created by the Channel spell. So Nancy cannot have Alfonso activate it at all during the Word of Command-forced casting of Squire, and cannot drain Alfonso's life this way. This card text controls over the general rule (723.5a) that a controlling player may use all of the controlled player's resources to pay costs.

Secondary points, assuming the timing given (Channel resolved earlier this turn, then Word of Command resolves and Nancy picks Squire from Alfonso's hand):

- Even if Channel were usable, Squire costs {1}{W}. Channel's {C} is colorless mana specifically and can pay the {1} generic portion, but it can never pay the {W}. So Alfonso would still need a white source, and only 1 generic mana is actually needed for the spell.
- Life payment limits: a player may pay life only if their life total is at least the amount paid (119.4/118.3), so 20 life from a 20-life total is technically a legal payment — but per Channel ruling #0, once a life total is 0 you can't pay any more life even if you haven't lost yet. A player at 0 or less life loses the game as a state-based action the next time a player would receive priority (119.6, 104.3b) — during Word of Command's resolution no one receives priority, so the loss would be checked afterward.
- Note also that Word of Command only compels Alfonso to play the chosen card if able; it does not compel him to activate mana abilities beyond what Nancy directs, and the mana produced must be spent on lands' mana abilities or on playing Squire, so pointless extra mana isn't sanctioned.

If instead Channel were cast after Word of Command started resolving, that's impossible — Alfonso is only being made to play Squire, and Nancy can't have him cast a different card (Word of Command ruling #3 limits it to the chosen card in hand).

This analysis involves just Nancy and Alfonso; the provided rules include a Two-Headed Giant note (810.9b) that if a cost lets both teammates pay life simultaneously, the total can't exceed the team's shared life total, but nothing here changes with more opponents at the table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. There is no restriction on how much mana Alfonso can add while casting Squire. While Word of Command does prevent Alfonso from activating mana abilities that aren't used to cast Squire, paying 1 life to add {C} due to Channel is not a mana ability, it is a special action.

entries.question: Aimee casts [Animate Dead] targeting [Scalebane's Elite] in their graveyard. What happens?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final outcome and sequence as the reference: Animate Dead returns Scalebane's Elite but cannot legally attach, is put into the graveyard as an unattached Aura, and its leaves-the-battlefield trigger causes the Elite to be sacrificed, leaving both in the graveyard.
entries.answer:
Scalebane's Elite comes back to the battlefield under Aimee's control, but Animate Dead can't attach to it (protection from black), so Animate Dead is immediately put into Aimee's graveyard as a state-based action, its leaves-the-battlefield trigger goes on the stack, and when that trigger resolves Aimee sacrifices Scalebane's Elite.

Step by step:
- Animate Dead targets a creature card in a graveyard, so it resolves and enters the battlefield attached to the Scalebane's Elite card in the graveyard [608.3c]. Protection from black is an ability that works only on the battlefield, so it doesn't stop the targeting or the initial attachment [Animate Dead ruling #4].
- Its enters trigger changes its enchant ability, returns Scalebane's Elite to the battlefield under Aimee's control, and tries to attach Animate Dead to it [Animate Dead ruling #1].
- Because Scalebane's Elite has protection from black on the battlefield, Animate Dead can't legally enchant it, so the attachment fails [303.4j, 701.3b].
- An Aura not attached to a legal object is put into its owner's graveyard as a state-based action [704.5m, 303.4c, 704.1]. That is a "when this Aura leaves the battlefield" event, so the delayed trigger triggers; on resolution, Scalebane's Elite (if still on the battlefield) is sacrificed by its controller, Aimee [Animate Dead ruling #0].

Net result: Aimee spent {1}{B}, briefly had a 4/4 Scalebane's Elite, and ends with both Animate Dead and Scalebane's Elite in the graveyard. This is the same in two-player and multiplayer games; nothing here depends on the number of opponents (though note an Aura also can't enchant something outside its controller's range of influence in games that use such a range [801.8]).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Both permanents end up in the graveyard.

Scalebane's Elite's protection ability doesn't function in the graveyard, so it's a legal target for Animate Dead. As Animate Dead's trigger resolves, first Animate Dead's enchant ability changes to "enchant creature put onto the battlefield with Animate Dead". Then Scalebane's Elite is returned to the battlefield. At this point the next instruction is to attach Animate Dead to Scalebane's Elite, but this is illegal to do because now that it's on the battlefield, Scalebane's Elite's protection ability is active.

After the triggered ability from Animate Dead has finished resolving, the game will check state-based actions and see that Animate Dead is an Aura that isn't enchanting anything, so it's put into its owner's graveyard.. This causes Animate Dead's leaves-the-battlefield ability to trigger, sacrificing Scalebane's Elite.

entries.question: Alondra controls an [Invasion of Ixalan] with 1 defense counter on it. They attack it with [Rankle and Torbran]. If they choose the second mode for Rankle and Torbran's triggered ability, could they sacrifice Invasion of Ixalan's back face [Belligerent Regisaur] to it?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Alondra can sacrifice Belligerent Regisaur only if they stack the triggers so Invasion of Ixalan's defeated-trigger resolves first, exiling and casting Regisaur before Rankle and Torbran's sacrifice mode resolves.
entries.answer:
Yes — potentially, but only if the timing lines up so that Belligerent Regisaur is already on the battlefield as a creature under Alondra's control when Rankle and Torbran's chosen mode resolves.

What happens: Rankle and Torbran (3/4, first strike) deals 3 combat damage to Invasion of Ixalan, which only has 1 defense counter left. Damage can legally be dealt to a battle [120.1a]. That reduces Invasion of Ixalan's defense to 0, but the state-based action that puts a 0-defense battle into its owner's graveyard is deliberately delayed while that battle is the source of an ability that has triggered and not yet left the stack [704.5v], and state-based actions don't use the stack [704.1]. Invasion of Ixalan's own reminder-text "when it's defeated" ability exiles it and then casts it transformed as Belligerent Regisaur; that card's printed text governs here.

So two things trigger off the same combat damage: Invasion of Ixalan's defeated trigger and Rankle and Torbran's "deals combat damage to a player or battle" trigger. Both are controlled by Alondra, so Alondra stacks them in the order they like. If Alondra puts Rankle and Torbran's trigger on the stack first and Invasion of Ixalan's defeated trigger on top, the defeated trigger resolves first, Invasion of Ixalan is exiled, and Belligerent Regisaur is cast; that spell is above Rankle and Torbran's trigger on the stack, so Belligerent Regisaur resolves and enters the battlefield as a 4/3 creature before the sacrifice mode resolves. At that point Alondra controls Belligerent Regisaur and may sacrifice it — sacrificing means its controller moves a permanent they control from the battlefield to its owner's graveyard [701.21a], and "a creature of their choice" lets each player pick.

If instead Alondra orders the triggers the other way (Rankle and Torbran's trigger resolving first), Belligerent Regisaur isn't on the battlefield yet and cannot be the sacrifice; Alondra would have to sacrifice some other creature (Rankle and Torbran itself, if it's the only one). Note also that Invasion of Ixalan while on the battlefield is a battle, not a creature, and can never be sacrificed as a creature or be an attacking/blocking creature [506.3f], [506.3g].

Multiplayer note: the second mode makes every player sacrifice a creature of their choice, so at a table of more than two the effect hits each opponent as well; a Siege's protector must be an opponent chosen as it enters [310.8a], [310.11], but that doesn't change the sacrifice answer.

One gap: the specific rules for choosing modes and for ordering simultaneous triggers you control weren't included in the context here, so treat the ordering step as the standard "you order your own triggers" procedure rather than something I can cite.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. When Rankle and Torbran attacks Invasion of Ixalan and removes the last defense counter from it, both Invasion of Ixalan and Rankle and Torbran's abilities will trigger. Alondra will get to choose the order in which the abilities go on the stack, so they could put Rankle and Torbran's triggered ability on the stack first with Invasion of Ixalan's triggered ability on top. Invasion of Ixalan's triggered ability will resolve first, so Invasion of Ixalan will be exiled and Alondra could choose to cast it transformed. When Rankle and Torbran's triggered ability resolves, Belligerent Regisaur will have resolved and be on the battlefield, so Alondra could choose to sacrifice it.

entries.question: Noah activates [Thespian's Stage] targeting a [Dark Depths] with ten ice counters on it. What happens?
entries.reason: The candidate misstates the timing/legend-rule interaction—claiming the copy is simply sacrificed and the original is "untouched"—whereas the correct ruling has a state trigger plus a legend choice/state-based action order that can affect which permanent is put into the graveyard before the trigger goes on the stack.
entries.answer:
Thespian's Stage becomes a copy of Dark Depths with zero ice counters on it, so Dark Depths's last ability (a state trigger) triggers immediately, and Noah sacrifices the copy to create Marit Lage — a legendary 20/20 black Avatar creature token with flying and indestructible. The original Dark Depths is untouched and keeps its ten ice counters.

Why: Thespian's Stage's ability copies only the printed copiable values of the target land; counters are not copied [Thespian's Stage ruling #3], and because Thespian's Stage is already on the battlefield, no "enters with" or "as this enters" effects apply — so "Dark Depths enters with ten ice counters on it" simply does nothing [Thespian's Stage ruling #1]. The copy is now a Dark Depths with no ice counters, and "When Dark Depths has no ice counters on it, sacrifice it" is a state trigger that triggers as soon as that condition is true [Dark Depths ruling #1]. On resolution Noah sacrifices it and creates the Marit Lage token.

Two notes:
- The copy retains Thespian's Stage's own copy ability ("except it has this ability"), but loses the {T}: Add {C} ability [Thespian's Stage ruling #0]. It also stays tapped from paying the {2}, {T} cost — it doesn't untap just because the copied land is untapped [Thespian's Stage ruling #2], and a permanent keeps its tapped status until something changes it [110.5c].
- If the copy somehow leaves the battlefield before the sacrifice trigger resolves (for example, it's bounced or destroyed in response), Noah can't sacrifice it and gets no Marit Lage [Dark Depths ruling #2]. Likewise, if the trigger is countered while the copy remains on the battlefield with no ice counters, it triggers again immediately [Dark Depths ruling #1].

Because both Dark Depths permanents are legendary, if Noah controls both, the "legend rule" would apply — but that's moot here since the copy is being sacrificed anyway. Nothing about this changes between a two-player and a multiplayer game; only Noah's own permanents are involved.

Then state-based actions are checked and Noah has to put either Dark Depths or Thespian's Stage into their graveyard. Then Thespian's Stage's trigger goes on the stack, and if Thespian's Stage is still on the battlefield during the resolution of the trigger, Noah sacrifices it and creates a 20/20 Marit Lage token.

entries.question: Ashley controls [Underworld Breach] and has [Reveillark] in their graveyard. Can they evoke it?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Ashley cannot evoke Reveillark because escape and evoke are alternative casting costs and only one may be used, so escape must be used to cast it from the graveyard.
entries.answer:
No. Ashley can cast Reveillark from their graveyard using the escape ability granted by Underworld Breach, but they can't apply Reveillark's evoke cost to that casting.

Why: Both escape and evoke are alternative costs — "You may cast this card from your graveyard by paying [cost] rather than paying its mana cost" for escape [702.138a], and "You may cast this spell by paying [cost] rather than paying its mana cost" for evoke [702.74a]. Rule 601.2b states plainly that a player can't apply two alternative methods of casting or two alternative costs to a single spell. Escape is the permission that lets Reveillark be cast from the graveyard at all here, so that alternative cost is the one being used, and evoke can't be substituted in on top of it.

So Ashley's actual cost is Reveillark's mana cost, {4}{W}, plus exiling three other cards from their graveyard (Underworld Breach sets the escape cost as "the card's mana cost plus exile three other cards from your graveyard"). Note the {W} is a colored symbol and must be paid with white mana; only the {4} is generic. That total is locked in per 601.2f.

Consequences: because Ashley did not choose to pay the evoke cost, evoke's triggered ability ("When this permanent enters, if its evoke cost was paid, its controller sacrifices it") does not trigger [702.74a, Reveillark ruling #5], so Reveillark stays on the battlefield. It will be a permanent that "escaped" [702.138b]. Timing is unchanged by either ability — Reveillark is a creature spell, so it's cast during a main phase when Ashley has priority and the stack is empty [Reveillark ruling #0].

This answer doesn't depend on the number of players; it's the same in a two-player or multiplayer game.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Escape and evoke are both alternative costs ([702.138a], [702.74a]), and Ashley may only pay one alternative cost for a spell. Since escape is the only thing that allows Ashley to cast Reveillark from their graveyard, they have to use that cost.

entries.question: Autumn controls [Slimefoot, the Stowaway] and a 1/1 Saproling token. Autumn casts [Deafening Clarion] choosing both modes. How much life does Autumn gain?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling that Autumn gains 2 life in a two-player game (and correctly explains the lifelink interaction and Slimefoot's triggered life gain).
entries.answer:
Autumn gains 2 life in a two-player game (and 1 + one life per opponent in multiplayer).

Breakdown:

1. Deafening Clarion's second mode gives creatures Autumn controls lifelink until end of turn, and both Slimefoot, the Stowaway and the 1/1 Saproling token are still on the battlefield to gain it even though the first mode's 3 damage is lethal to each of them [Deafening Clarion ruling #1].
2. The 3 damage from the first mode does NOT gain Autumn any life. Lifelink only gains life for damage dealt *by the source with lifelink* [702.15b, 120.3f]. The source of that damage is Deafening Clarion (a sorcery), which has no lifelink; the creatures that have lifelink aren't dealing it.
3. Both the Saproling token and Slimefoot, the Stowaway are destroyed by the 3 damage simultaneously. The Saproling's death still triggers Slimefoot, the Stowaway's ability: "Whenever a Saproling you control dies, Slimefoot deals 1 damage to each opponent and you gain 1 life."
4. When that trigger resolves: the "you gain 1 life" clause gains Autumn 1 life. Additionally, Slimefoot, the Stowaway is the source of the 1 damage dealt to each opponent, and it had lifelink from Deafening Clarion, so Autumn gains 1 more life per opponent dealt damage [702.15b, 120.3f].

So with one opponent: 1 (Slimefoot's own clause) + 1 (lifelink) = 2 life. At a multiplayer table with three opponents it would be 1 + 3 = 4 life, since Slimefoot deals 1 damage to each opponent.

These are separate life-gain events, not one lump gain, so anything like Ajani's Pridemate that triggers on gaining life would trigger once per event [702.15e, 119.9].

Timing note: I'm assuming the standard reading that Deafening Clarion's damage mode and lifelink mode both apply as the single spell resolves, with lifelink granted to the creatures before they leave the battlefield [Deafening Clarion ruling #1]. Only creatures Autumn controls as Deafening Clarion resolves gain lifelink [Deafening Clarion ruling #0]; if the Saproling had entered after resolution, the damage math would be unchanged but nothing would have lifelink, leaving only the 1 life from Slimefoot's ability.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Two.

Deafening Clarion deals three damage to each creature, then gives them lifelink. After the spell has resolved, state-based actions are checked and both creatures die. Slimefoot, the Stowaway's ability is a leave-the-battlefield trigger, so it sees that it existed immediately before Slimefoot, the Stowaway died and therefore triggers. When it resolves, it sees that Slimefoot, the Stowaway had lifelink right before it died, so Autumn gains 1 life from the damage that's dealt to Noor.

entries.question: Ace controls [Soul Warden] and casts [Realmwalker]. Can Natalie kill it before Ace casts a creature from the top of their library?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling as the reference: opponents get priority after Realmwalker enters (and while Soul Warden’s trigger is on the stack), so Natalie can destroy it before Ace can use its ability to cast the top card.
entries.answer:
Yes. Natalie gets at least one priority window in which Realmwalker is on the battlefield and Ace has not yet cast anything off the top of their library, so she can kill Realmwalker first.

How the timing works:

1. Ace casts Realmwalker. Because Ace had priority before casting it, Ace receives priority again immediately after Realmwalker becomes cast [601.2i]. Natalie can respond then (a counterspell etc.) [117.7].
2. Once all players pass, Realmwalker (top object of the stack) resolves and enters the battlefield [608.1]. Ace chooses a creature type as it enters. Soul Warden's ability ("Whenever another creature enters, you gain 1 life") triggers, but nothing happens at the moment it triggers; it is put on the stack the next time a player would receive priority [117.2a].
3. That next time is right after Realmwalker finishes resolving: Soul Warden's trigger goes on the stack and Ace gets priority. Ace cannot cast a creature spell from the top of their library at that moment, because Realmwalker "doesn't change when you can cast creature spells" — Ace needs their own main phase with an empty stack (absent flash) [Realmwalker ruling #3]. So the Soul Warden trigger must resolve first, and Natalie has priority windows both with that trigger on the stack and after it resolves. She can destroy/exile/bounce Realmwalker in one of those windows.
4. If Realmwalker leaves the battlefield before Ace casts, Ace loses the permission entirely and can't cast the top card. Note Ace's life gain from Soul Warden still happens regardless, since the trigger is independent of Realmwalker's continued presence.

One nuance: no player receives priority during the resolution of a spell, and if some effect had Ace cast a spell during a resolution, no player would get priority after that cast [608.2g] — but nothing here does that.

Multiplayer: the same answer holds with more than two players; any opponent, not just Natalie, may act in these windows, and simultaneous choices/priority pass in turn order (APNAP) [616.1f].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. When Realmwalker enters the battlefield Soul Warden's trigger will go on the stack, at which point both players will have a chance to respond.

entries.question: Alondra has 10 life and Nico has 20 life. Alondra attacks Nico with [Kaalia of the Vast] and puts in [Scourge of the Throne]. Will they get an extra combat phase?
entries.reason: The candidate declines to give the ruling and fails to state that Scourge of the Throne's "Whenever this creature attacks..." trigger does not occur when it's put onto the battlefield attacking.
entries.answer:
I can't settle this with the rules provided. The whole question turns on whether a creature that is put onto the battlefield attacking (rather than declared as an attacker) triggers an ability that reads "Whenever this creature attacks...", and no rule in the context above addresses that point.

What the provided material does establish:

- Kaalia of the Vast's ability puts an Angel, Demon, or Dragon from your hand onto the battlefield tapped and attacking the opponent Kaalia of the Vast attacked — so Scourge of the Throne is never declared as an attacker in the declare attackers step [Kaalia of the Vast ruling #1].
- Scourge of the Throne's own text has an intervening "if" clause: it must be attacking the player with the most life (or tied) both when it's declared as an attacker and again as the ability starts to resolve, or the ability does nothing at all [Scourge of the Throne ruling #2]. Nico at 20 life is the player with the most life, so the life-total part of that condition is satisfied here; the sticking point is the "when it's declared as an attacker" part, since Scourge of the Throne was put onto the battlefield attacking instead of being declared.
- If Scourge of the Throne's ability did trigger and resolve with its condition met, its text would untap all attacking creatures and give Alondra an additional combat phase after this phase; per rule 500.10 an effect that adds a phase creates that phase directly after the current one, and per rule 506.7c/506.7d spells restricted to a point "in the combat phase" apply per combat phase as described there.

What's missing: the rule governing whether "put onto the battlefield attacking" counts as "attacking" for the purposes of an "attacks" trigger (the rule usually cited is in the declare attackers section, which isn't in the context). Without it I won't guess.

This analysis doesn't depend on the number of players; none of the provided rules change based on two players versus more, though with more than two players Kaalia of the Vast must have attacked the specific opponent, and "the player with the most life" is checked across all players.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Scourge of the Throne has a triggered ability that occurs only when it is declared as an attacking creature. It was put onto the battlefield attacking, which doesn't meet its trigger condition.

entries.question: Alma deals combat damage to Nico with their [Ragavan, Nimble Pilferer]. They exile [Deceit] from Nico's library. Can Alma evoke Deceit?
entries.reason: Both the candidate and the reference conclude Ragavan's effect allows Alma to cast Deceit from exile this turn and that Alma may cast it using its evoke alternative cost.
entries.answer:
Yes. Ragavan, Nimble Pilferer's ability says "Until end of turn, you may cast that card," which is an effect permitting Alma to cast Deceit from exile. Evoke is "a static ability that functions in any zone from which the card with evoke can be cast" (702.74a), so once Ragavan, Nimble Pilferer makes Deceit castable from exile, Deceit's evoke ability applies there too and Alma may pay {U/B}{U/B} (two mana, each either blue or black) instead of Deceit's mana cost of {4}{U/B}{U/B}. Casting for evoke follows the alternative-cost rules in 601.2b and 601.2f\u2014h, so Alma announces the use of the evoke alternative cost as they cast it and may not combine it with another alternative method of casting. Note Alma must still cast Deceit within the duration Ragavan, Nimble Pilferer grants (this turn) and at a legal time for a creature spell (their own main phase with an empty stack, absent other effects).

When Deceit enters the battlefield, evoke's triggered ability triggers and Alma sacrifices it (702.74a). Its enters-the-battlefield triggers still go on the stack alongside that sacrifice trigger: if Alma spent {U}{U} on the total cost, Deceit's first ability can return a nonland permanent to its owner's hand; if Alma spent {B}{B}, an opponent reveals their hand and discards a card Alma chooses. Deceit ruling #0 confirms those abilities look at what mana was spent for the whole cost, not just the hybrid symbols \u2014 and here the entire evoke cost is those two hybrid symbols, so paying both with blue triggers the first ability, both with black triggers the second, and one of each triggers neither.

One detail on the effect finding the card: because Ragavan, Nimble Pilferer's effect allows a nonland card to be cast, the rest of that effect can track the object after it moves to the stack (400.7h), so nothing about the zone change breaks the permission. This works the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table \u2014 the exile and casting permission relate only to the player Ragavan, Nimble Pilferer damaged (Nico) and to Alma; with more players, Deceit's second ability's "target opponent" simply gives Alma a choice among opponents.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Ragavan, Nimble Pilferer's trigger creates a continuous effect that lets Alma cast Deceit this turn, with no restrictions on how it's cast. Alma is free to cast Deceit for its alternative cost by evoking it.

entries.question: Amiyah taps their [The One Ring], which currently has no burden counters on it, to draw a card. Before that resolves Nico casts [Soul Partition] targeting The One Ring. How many cards does Amiyah draw when the activated ability resolves?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling (Amiyah draws zero) and uses the same reasoning that the Ring is exiled so no burden counter can be placed and last known information shows zero counters.
entries.answer:
Amiyah draws zero cards.

The activated ability of The One Ring exists on the stack independently of The One Ring itself, so exiling The One Ring with Soul Partition does not counter the ability — it still resolves (rule 113.7a). Note the ability doesn't target anything, so there's no illegal-target check that would stop it (608.2b).

On resolution, the controller follows the instructions in order (608.2c): first "put a burden counter on The One Ring." The One Ring is no longer on the battlefield, so no counter can be put on it. Then "draw a card for each burden counter on The One Ring" uses The One Ring's last known information from the battlefield (113.7a), which was zero burden counters. Zero counters means zero cards drawn.

Timing assumption: Soul Partition resolved and exiled The One Ring before the activated ability resolved (that's what "before that resolves" describes). If instead the activated ability resolved first, Amiyah would put a burden counter on The One Ring and draw 1 card, and Soul Partition would then exile it.

This analysis is the same regardless of the number of players; the only multiplayer wrinkle from the provided card text is that if Nico (an opponent of Amiyah) later casts The One Ring from exile via Soul Partition, it costs {2} more.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: None. When The One Ring's ability resolves it can't put a burden counter on The One Ring because it's no longer on the battlefield. The game uses its last known information to determine how many burden counters were on The One Ring before it was exiled.

entries.question: Nathaniel controls [Rest in Peace] and [Dauthi Voidwalker], and Armani casts [Read the Bones]. What happens to it?
entries.reason: Both answers say Armani chooses which replacement effect applies and Read the Bones is exiled either way, with that choice determining whether it gets a void counter.
entries.answer:
Read the Bones resolves normally (Armani scries 2, draws two cards, loses 2 life), and then, instead of going to Armani's graveyard, Read the Bones is exiled. Armani — as the card's owner, since a spell on the stack heading to the graveyard has no controller once it finishes resolving — chooses which of the two replacement effects applies (616.1, 616.1f, 400.6).

Both Rest in Peace ("If a card or token would be put into a graveyard from anywhere, exile it instead") and Dauthi Voidwalker ("If a card would be put into an opponent's graveyard from anywhere, instead exile it with a void counter on it") are replacement effects trying to modify the same event — Read the Bones being put into Armani's graveyard (614.1). Neither is a self-replacement effect and neither changes control of a permanent entering the battlefield, so no effect is forced to be chosen first; the choice is free (614.15, 616.1a, 616.1b, 616.1e).

- If Armani picks Rest in Peace, Read the Bones is exiled with no counter, and the process repeats — but the graveyard event no longer happens, so Dauthi Voidwalker's effect does nothing (614.7, 616.1f).
- If Armani picks Dauthi Voidwalker, Read the Bones is exiled with a void counter on it, and Nathaniel can later tap and sacrifice Dauthi Voidwalker to cast Read the Bones without paying its mana cost that turn (subject to normal timing rules for sorceries).

So Armani will essentially always choose Rest in Peace, denying Nathaniel the void counter. Note Dauthi Voidwalker only applies because Armani is Nathaniel's opponent; Rest in Peace applies to everyone's cards.

Multiplayer note: this works the same at any number of players. If several players' cards were being put into graveyards simultaneously and multiple owners had to choose, those choices are made in APNAP order (101.4, 616.1).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Armani gets to choose which replacement effect applies to it. After applying that effect, it's no longer moving to the graveyard, so the other effect doesn't apply. It'll end up in exile either way, but Armani gets to choose whether it has a void counter on it.

entries.question: Aspen control [Pulmonic Sliver]. They cast [Dihada's Ploy], discarding [Dregscape Sliver] on resolution. Can Aspen put Dregscape Sliver on top of their library?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude no; Pulmonic Sliver's replacement effect only applies to Sliver permanents on the battlefield and cannot replace a Sliver card being discarded from hand.
entries.answer:
No. Dregscape Sliver goes to Aspen's graveyard as normal.

Two reasons, both from Pulmonic Sliver's own text: (1) Pulmonic Sliver's static abilities affect Slivers on the battlefield, so a Sliver card sitting in Aspen's hand isn't granted the ability at all; and (2) even the wording of the granted ability, "If this permanent would be put into a graveyard, you may put it on top of its owner's library instead," only applies to a permanent. A card in hand is not a permanent — it's just a card — so discarding Dregscape Sliver from hand isn't a permanent being put into a graveyard and the replacement effect has nothing to replace. (Compare Pulmonic Sliver ruling #3, which frames the effect around Slivers that would die, i.e. be put into a graveyard from the battlefield.) Card text controls here, and it simply doesn't cover discards.

Assumed timing: Dihada's Ploy's own instruction "Draw two cards, then discard a card" happens during its resolution, and Aspen chooses Dregscape Sliver then. Note that no player receives priority in the middle of a spell's resolution, so Aspen can't take actions between the draws and the discard (117.1, 608.1, 608.2n); the discard just happens, and Dregscape Sliver lands in the graveyard.

Upside: that discarded Dregscape Sliver counts toward Dihada's Ploy's life gain (Dihada's Ploy ruling #0 — it counts the card discarded as part of its effect, plus any discarded earlier this turn, including a jump-start discard if Aspen cast it from the graveyard). And once Dregscape Sliver is in the graveyard it's not on the battlefield, so per Dregscape Sliver ruling #2 it isn't granting unearth to other Sliver cards from there — though its own printed unearth {2} still lets Aspen return Dregscape Sliver itself from the graveyard.

This answer doesn't depend on player count; it's the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Pulmonic Sliver's ability affects only Sliver permanents on the battlefield, and not Sliver cards in other zones.

entries.question: Arely controls a [Barony Vampire]. Nico controls a [Trained Jackal]. Arely casts [Prey Upon], targeting the Barony Vampire and Trained Jackal. In response, Nico casts [Hanabi Blast], targeting the Barony Vampire. What happens?
entries.reason: Both conclude Hanabi Blast resolves first and kills Barony Vampire, and Prey Upon then resolves but its fight does nothing so Trained Jackal takes no damage.
entries.answer:
Hanabi Blast resolves first and kills Barony Vampire, and then Prey Upon does nothing at all.

Step by step:

1. Nico's Hanabi Blast was cast while Prey Upon was already on the stack, so it resolves first [117.7]. It deals 2 damage to Barony Vampire, a 3/2, which is lethal, so Barony Vampire dies and goes to Arely's graveyard.
2. As part of Hanabi Blast's own resolution, Hanabi Blast returns to its owner's hand and then its controller (Nico, assuming Nico owns it) discards a card at random. If Arely owned that Hanabi Blast, it would return to Arely's hand and Nico would still be the one discarding at random [Hanabi Blast ruling #0].
3. Prey Upon then tries to resolve. Barony Vampire is no longer on the battlefield, so it is an illegal target — a target that no longer exists or no longer meets the spell's specifications [Illegal Target] [608.2b]. Trained Jackal is still a legal target, but Prey Upon requires both.
4. Because one of Prey Upon's targets is illegal on resolution, no creature deals or is dealt damage [Prey Upon ruling #0]. Trained Jackal is untouched and survives. (Note that under 608.2b a spell only fails to resolve entirely if *all* its targets are illegal; here Trained Jackal is still legal, so Prey Upon does resolve but its fight instruction accomplishes nothing per its ruling.) Prey Upon is then put into Arely's graveyard as the final part of its resolution [608.2n].

Timing assumption: the question says Hanabi Blast was cast "in response," so it is above Prey Upon on the stack and resolves first. If instead Nico had somehow only cast Hanabi Blast after Prey Upon finished resolving, Prey Upon's fight would have happened first — Barony Vampire and Trained Jackal would deal 3 and 1 damage to each other, killing Trained Jackal, and Hanabi Blast's 2 damage would then finish off Barony Vampire.

Nothing here depends on the number of players; the result is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: The Hanabi Blast resolves, removing the Barony Vampire from the battlefield. Prey Upon resolves, but no damage is dealt to the Trained Jackal.

entries.question: Annabel controls [Altar of Dementia] and casts [Too Greedily, Too Deep] returning Nolan's [Sepulchral Primordial] to the battlefield. Can Annabel use Altar of Dementia to sacrifice Sepulchral Primordial and return it to the battlefield using its own triggered ability?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Annabel cannot have Sepulchral Primordial target itself because its ETB trigger's targets are chosen while the creature is on the battlefield, so it isn't a legal target.
entries.answer:
No. Sepulchral Primordial cannot bring itself back with its own enters-the-battlefield trigger.

Why: Too Greedily, Too Deep puts Sepulchral Primordial onto the battlefield under Annabel's control, and its triggered ability ("When this creature enters, for each opponent, you may put up to one target creature card from that player's graveyard onto the battlefield under your control") triggers. Targets for a triggered ability are chosen when the ability is put on the stack, which happens the next time a player would receive priority — and at that moment Sepulchral Primordial is on the battlefield, not in anyone's graveyard, so it is not a legal target [113.7a]. There is no window in which Annabel can activate Altar of Dementia ("Sacrifice a creature: Target player mills cards equal to the sacrificed creature's power") before the trigger's targets are locked in, because she only gets priority after the trigger is already on the stack with its targets chosen.

If Annabel instead sacrifices Sepulchral Primordial to Altar of Dementia after the trigger is on the stack (putting the card into Nolan's graveyard, since a card goes to its owner's graveyard), that does nothing to help: the trigger will resolve doing only what it can for the targets it already has, and it cannot pick up a card that wasn't targeted [603.6]. Zone-change triggers look for objects in the zone the object moved to, and a card that changes zones becomes a new object with no relation to its earlier existence [400.7], so nothing retroactively makes Sepulchral Primordial a target.

Multiplayer note: with more than two players, "for each opponent" lets Annabel choose one target creature card in each opponent's graveyard, including Nolan's — but the same restriction applies, since Sepulchral Primordial isn't in a graveyard when targets are chosen. In a two-player game only Nolan's graveyard is eligible. In either case Annabel could sacrifice a different creature to Altar of Dementia and mill Nolan, but Sepulchral Primordial still can't reanimate itself.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Annabel must choose a target for Sepulchral Primordial's triggered ability as it is put onto the stack. At this time, Sepulchral Primordial is still on the battlefield.

entries.question: Ari casts [Memories Returning]. Does Noor have a chance to exile it with [Dawnhand Dissident] before Ari can cast Memories Returning again for its flashback cost?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Noor cannot exile Memories Returning before Ari casts it with flashback because after it resolves the active player gets priority and can cast it from the graveyard before opponents can act.
entries.answer:
No — assuming Ari has the mana and casts it right away, Noor gets no window. Ari can cast Memories Returning from the graveyard for its Flashback {7}{U}{U} before Noor ever receives priority.

Why:

1. While Memories Returning is on the stack the first time, Dawnhand Dissident's "{T}, Blight 2: Exile target card from a graveyard" has no legal target for it — Memories Returning is a spell on the stack, not a card in a graveyard (a spell is a card on the stack, [112.1]). Noor can respond to the spell ([117.7]), but not exile it.
2. Memories Returning resolves and is put into Ari's graveyard. Ari, as the player whose turn it is, receives priority at that point before any opponent can act — Memories Returning ruling #2 states this directly: "If a card with flashback is put into your graveyard during your turn, you can cast it if it's legal to do so before any other player can take any actions." With priority ([117.1a]) and an empty stack in Ari's main phase (flashback still obeys sorcery timing, Memories Returning ruling #0), Ari legally casts it from the graveyard by paying {7}{U}{U} instead of {2}{U}{U} ([702.34a], Memories Returning ruling #4). Once it's cast, Ari keeps priority ([601.2i]).
3. Now Memories Returning is on the stack again and again untargetable by Dawnhand Dissident's exile ability. And it won't matter: a spell cast with flashback is exiled no matter how it leaves the stack (Memories Returning ruling #3).

When Noor DOES get a chance: if Ari can't or doesn't cast it immediately and passes priority, or if Ari's main phase has ended, or Ari casts something else first, then Noor may activate "{T}, Blight 2" while Memories Returning sits in Ari's graveyard and exile it, denying the flashback. Note Dawnhand Dissident's last ability (casting creature spells from exile during your turn) is irrelevant here — Memories Returning is a sorcery.

Timing assumption: I read the question as Ari intending to flash it back at the first opportunity in the same main phase. If instead Ari waits (e.g., taps out, or the turn moves on), Noor's window opens as described above.

Two players vs. more: the answer is the same at any table size. Ari, the active player, receives priority first after Memories Returning resolves, so no opponent — whether one or several — gets to act in between ([117.1a], Memories Returning ruling #2).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
No. After Memories Returning resolves, Ari receives priority.. At this point, Memories Returning is in the graveyard, and they can choose to cast it again. When it's cast, it goes from the graveyard to the stack. Noor does not receive priority until after Memories Returning is on the stack, so Memories Returning can't be exiled with Dawnhand Dissident.

(Unless there's something else on the battlefield that would create a triggered ability when Memories Returning resolves. In that case, Ari wouldn't be able to cast Memories Returning until the trigger has left the stack, and Noor could exile it in response to the trigger.)

entries.question: Aubrey and Arely are playing 2HG. Aubrey attacks with [Coral Commando] and Arely casts [Flash Conscription] to gain control of Coral Commando after it's been declared as an attacker in the declare attackers step. Is it still attacking?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Arely gaining control of Coral Commando removes it from combat so it stops being an attacking creature, even in Two-Headed Giant.
entries.answer:
No — Coral Commando stops attacking. Gaining control of an attacking creature removes it from combat: a permanent is removed from combat if its controller changes, and a creature removed from combat stops being an attacking, blocking, blocked, and/or unblocked creature [506.4a]. So when Flash Conscription resolves and Arely takes control of Coral Commando, Coral Commando is no longer an attacking creature, deals no combat damage in the combat damage step, and any blocker assigned to it becomes blocking nothing.

This is true even though Aubrey and Arely are teammates in Two-Headed Giant. In shared team turns, the active team declares one combined attack and announces what each creature is attacking [805.10b], but control is still tracked per player, not per team, so a teammate taking control of Coral Commando is a controller change and triggers removal from combat [506.4a].

A few knock-on points:
- Coral Commando already "attacked" for purposes of any abilities that triggered on attackers being declared; those triggers happened at declaration and are unaffected [508.2a], [508.3c]. Removing it from combat later doesn't undo them.
- Spells or abilities that would have kept Coral Commando from attacking wouldn't remove it from combat, but a control change specifically does [506.4a].
- Timing assumption: I'm reading Flash Conscription as cast after attackers were declared (during the declare attackers step, once the active player had priority [508.2a]). If instead it were cast before attackers were declared, Arely would simply control Coral Commando, and since a creature can only attack if its controller is an attacking player, it would be Arely's creature to declare (in 2HG, part of the team's combined attack) rather than being removed from combat.
- Untapping and haste from Flash Conscription don't put Coral Commando back into combat; nothing here states it's attacking, which is what would be required to make it an attacking creature again [508.4].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. A creature that changes controllers is removed from combat. Even though Aubrey and Arely are on the same team and are both allowed to be attacking with creatures, they are different players and therefore Arely gaining control of Aubrey's creature still qualifies as a control change.

entries.question: Axel controls [Vastwood Gorger] and attacks Nico's [Teferi, Who Slows the Sunset]. Before damage is dealt, Nico activates [Barrin, Master Wizard], sacrificing Teferi, Who Slows the Sunset. Does Vastwood Gorger deal damage? If so, to what?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that once Teferi is sacrificed and removed from combat the attacking Vastwood Gorger is attacking nothing and therefore assigns no combat damage.
entries.answer:
Vastwood Gorger deals no combat damage at all (assuming it is unblocked and stays on the battlefield).

When Teferi, Who Slows the Sunset is sacrificed as part of the cost of Barrin, Master Wizard's ability, it leaves the battlefield and is therefore removed from combat — a permanent removed from combat has no further involvement in that combat phase [506.4], [Remove from Combat]. Removing the attacked planeswalker does not remove Vastwood Gorger from combat: Vastwood Gorger continues to be an attacking creature, but it is attacking no player, planeswalker, or battle, it may still be blocked, and if it is unblocked it deals no combat damage [506.4c]. The combat damage rules confirm this: an unblocked creature assigns damage to the player, planeswalker, or battle it's attacking, and if it isn't currently attacking anything — for example, because the planeswalker it was attacking left the battlefield — it assigns no combat damage [510.1b].

Vastwood Gorger has no trample, so none of its damage can be redirected to Nico; rule [702.19f] states that a creature without trample over planeswalkers that was attacking a planeswalker can assign no combat damage to the defending player even if that planeswalker has been removed from combat. (Only "trample over planeswalkers" would let the damage go to Nico, and even then it would not count as attacking Nico [702.19e].)

Timing note: I'm assuming Barrin, Master Wizard's ability resolves before the combat damage step. If instead combat damage had already been dealt to Teferi, Who Slows the Sunset, that damage would have counted and the sacrifice afterward would change nothing about the damage already dealt. Also note Barrin, Master Wizard's ability returns a target *creature* to its owner's hand; if Nico targeted Vastwood Gorger itself, Vastwood Gorger would leave the battlefield and likewise be removed from combat and deal no damage [506.4].

This works the same whether it's a two-player game or a multiplayer game; the relevant "defending player" is determined per attacking creature as the controller of the planeswalker it was attacking [508.5].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No, Vastwood Gorger does not deal any combat damage. When combat damage would be assigned, a creature that is not currently attacking anything does not deal combat damage.
